#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.4 — Open the acquired repository with gix's isolated permissions

- Opened: `pending` by `.7.2`'s split (DOC-0026); `R-44-45-4` clause 5, the second ATTACHED clause.
- The finding: `git.rs:736` calls `gix::init_bare(target_dir)`, i.e. `ThreadSafeRepository::init(…, create::Options::default())`, so the operator's global and system git configuration and the git environment variables are honoured while fetching a caller-supplied URL. gix 0.87.1 ships the named remedy it does not use — `open::Options::isolated()`, whose own doc is *"prevent accessing anything else than the repository configuration file, prohibiting accessing the environment or spreading beyond the git repository location"* — against §12.5's "default refusal of submodules, hooks, filters, alternates, and external diff/clean drivers".
- ⛔ **Distinct from `.7.2.1`**, which owned the workspace DIRECTORY and closed the locality half of the same record sentence. This is about what gix READS, and an owned directory does not bound it.
- ⚠️ The census owed before the fix: WHICH of those configuration sources the acquisition path actually consults today. `isolated()` is the remedy the dependency names, but a repair that swaps it in without measuring what changes is the shape `.3.4.1` had to reverse — the leaf must know what it is turning off.
- Owns: that census, then the isolated open, then a control that proves an operator-level git setting no longer reaches the acquisition.
- Acceptance: the census names each configuration source the current path consults, by command; the repository is opened with permissions that exclude the environment and anything outside the repository location; a control sets a global or environment git setting that today changes acquisition behaviour and shows it no longer does; and the existing acquisition suites pass unchanged.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0207.
- **THE CENSUS, OWED BEFORE THE FIX, read out of gix 0.87.1's OWN SOURCE under `.project-data/cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-*/gix-0.87.1/` rather than from its release notes.** Three commands establish what the acquisition was opening with:
  - `sed -n '341,343p' gix-0.87.1/src/lib.rs` → `init_bare` is `ThreadSafeRepository::init(directory, create::Kind::Bare, create::Options::default())`.
  - `sed -n '53,57p' gix-0.87.1/src/init.rs` → that `init` builds `crate::open::Options::default_for_level(gix_sec::Trust::Full)`.
  - `sed -n '212,219p' gix-0.87.1/src/open/permissions.rs` → `Trust::Full => Permissions::all()`.
- **What `Permissions::all()` admits, and what `isolated()` turns off — each row read from `gix-0.87.1/src/open/permissions.rs` and each gate from `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs`:**

| Source | `gix::init_bare` | isolated | The gate, by line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the repository's own `config` | loaded | **loaded** | gix always loads it — *"configuration from inside of the repository is always loaded as it's definitely required for correctness"* |
| system config `$(prefix)/etc/gitconfig` | `system: true` | `false` | `Config { system: use_system, .. }`, `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:229` |
| application config `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config`, else `$HOME/.config/git/config` | `git: true` | `false` | `git: use_git`, `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:230` |
| user config `~/.gitconfig` | `user: true` | `false` | `user: use_user`, `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:231` |
| environment config `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n` | `env: true` | `false` | `env: use_env`, `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:232`; consumed at `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:300` — `if use_env { globals.append(gix_config::File::from_env(options)?…) }` |
| `include` / `includeIf` directives | `includes: true` | `false` | `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:243` — `if use_includes { …follow(…) } else { …no_follow() }` |
| system + application `gitattributes` | `Attributes::all()` | `Attributes::isolated()` | `src/open/permissions.rs` |
| every `GIT_*`/`SSH_*` category (`home`, `xdg_config_home`, `http_transport`, `identity`, `objects`, `git_prefix`, `ssh_prefix`) | `Environment::all()`, all `Allow` | all `Deny` | `gix-0.87.1/src/config/cache/init.rs:394` — the `core.*`/`gitoxide.*` env overrides are `if use_repository_local_environment { git_prefix } else { Permission::Deny }`, and `git_prefix` is `Deny` under isolation |
| the `git` binary's own configuration | `git_binary: false` | `false` | ⛔ **off in BOTH** — the leaf must not claim this as something the repair turned off |

- ⚠️ **Two option differences the census found that are NOT permissions, named rather than discovered later.** `Options::isolated()` is `Options::default().permissions(Permissions::isolated())`, and `Options::default()` differs from `default_for_level(Trust::Full)` in exactly two fields: `git_dir_trust: None` (⭐ irrelevant here — `init_opts` overwrites it with `Some(Trust::Full)` at `gix-0.87.1/src/init.rs:76`) and `filter_config_section: None` instead of `Some(config::section::is_trusted)`. The second filters config sections by the trust of the file they came from; under isolation the ONLY file loaded is the repository's own config, which this process created one call earlier, so the filter has nothing left to exclude. `lenient_config` is `true` in both, so a malformed config is still tolerated rather than becoming a new failure mode.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCED AT RUNTIME BEFORE THE REPAIR, and the leak is not theoretical.** With the opener reverted to `gix::init_bare`, `a_git_setting_in_the_environment_cannot_reach_the_acquisition` fails at `the setting must not reach the acquisition's own open`, and the probe's own output is the evidence: `default-permissions HEAD: ref: refs/heads/smuggled` AND `acquisition HEAD: ref: refs/heads/smuggled`. A git setting supplied purely through the server process's ENVIRONMENT reached the repository the acquisition creates for a caller-supplied URL.
- ⭐ **THE INSTRUMENT IS A CHILD PROCESS, and choosing it is the real design decision.** `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0` cannot be set in-process: `libtest` runs this binary's tests in parallel threads and Rust makes `set_var` unsafe for exactly that reason, so a mutation would reach every other test in the binary. The control therefore re-executes its own test binary with `--exact git::tests::the_git_environment_probe --include-ignored --nocapture` and the setting in `Command::env`, so it is in place BEFORE the process starts and nothing is mutated. ⛔ The probe is `#[ignore]`d with a reason naming its parent — a skip that explains itself, per `.11.4.7.2.4`'s lesson that an invisible skip reads like a pass; the run prints `1 ignored` with that sentence.
- ⭐ **It is a MATCHED PAIR in one process, which is what makes a green result mean something** (`docs/knowledge/a-falsification-you-can-leave-behind.md`). The probe opens one repository the superseded way and one the way production does, under the SAME environment, and prints both. The first must say `refs/heads/smuggled` — proving the setting really arrives on this host — and the second must say `refs/heads/main`. ⛔ Without the first half, a repair that broke the environment plumbing entirely would look identical to one that refused it.
- **The repair.** `acquire_into` calls a named `init_acquisition_repository`, which is `gix::ThreadSafeRepository::init_opts(dir, create::Kind::Bare, create::Options::default(), gix::open::Options::isolated())`. ⭐ `isolated()` is the remedy the dependency itself names, and its doc is the acceptance in gix's own words: *"prevent accessing anything else than the repository configuration file, prohibiting accessing the environment or spreading beyond the git repository location"*.
- ⛔ **This is what `.7.2.1` could not reach, and saying so is the point.** That leaf owned the workspace DIRECTORY — exclusive creation, mode 0700, on the repository volume. Owning WHERE gix writes says nothing about WHAT gix reads, and the record's sentence carried both.
- ✅ **The module header is updated in the same commit**, so R1's doc says what its call graph now performs — the shape `.7.2.2` had to repair in this same file.
- ⚠️ **Not claimed:** the HTTP transport is `ClassifiedGitHttp`, a custom `gix_transport` client, so `http.*` configuration never reached the dial in the first place and this repair does not change that. What it changes is the repository open.
- 🔎 **ROUTED, not reported: the FIXTURES still open with `Permissions::all()`.** `git.rs`'s test repositories are built with `gix::init(...)` at four sites, so the suite that proves this repair still reads the host's system, application and user git configuration to build its own inputs. It changes no assertion today — the fixtures assert commit ids and counts, and `acquire_local` resolves through the advertised `HEAD` — but a suite whose inputs vary with the operator's `~/.gitconfig` is host-dependent by construction. New owner with its own acceptance: `.7.2.5`.
- Verification: `python3 -B scripts/project_env.py cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --lib --locked` rc=0, **109 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored**, the acquisition suite unchanged at 12 passed (`the_acquisition_resolves_the_commit_and_measures`, `the_receipt_carries_the_commit_the_digest_and_the_manifest`, `the_budget_ceilings_trip_with_their_names`, `the_submodule_and_lfs_entries_refuse_with_their_names` and both `.7.2.2` redirect controls all pass). `cargo clippy -p reasonbraid-server --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` rc=0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` rc=0; `make gate` rc=0; `mdbook build docs/book` and `scripts/check_book_links.sh` rc=0.
- **FALSIFIED, self-reversing, and proved restored:** reverting `init_acquisition_repository` to `gix::init_bare(dir)` reproduces the RED above (`test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed`); restoring the file and `cmp -s` against the pre-neutralization copy reports byte-identical; the positive control afterwards is 109 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored.
- promotion: declined (the transferable halves are already recorded — `a-falsification-you-can-leave-behind` for the matched pair, `a-pin-a-second-path-can-bypass-is-not-a-pin` for the skip that must say so. What is new is the census table itself, which is gix-version-specific and belongs in the book, where it now is).

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.5 — The acquisition fixtures build their inputs under the host's git configuration

- Opened: `pending` by `.7.2.4`, which measured it and deliberately did not absorb it.
- The finding: `git.rs`'s test repositories are created with `gix::init(...)` — `Permissions::all()`, the same default `.7.2.4` just removed from production — at four sites (`source_repo`, the submodule fixture, the LFS fixture, `one_blob_repo`), plus `gix::init_bare` inside `the_git_environment_probe`, where it is DELIBERATE and must stay: it is the matched pair's other half.
- ⚠️ **State it at its real width.** No assertion changes today: the fixtures assert commit ids, file counts, depths and refusal names, and `acquire_local` resolves through the advertised `HEAD` rather than a branch name. What is wrong is that the suite's INPUTS are a function of the operator's `~/.gitconfig`, `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/config`, `$(prefix)/etc/gitconfig` and `GIT_*` environment — so the same commit can build different fixtures on two machines, and the difference would surface as an unexplained failure rather than as a named one.
- ⛔ Not a security defect and the leaf must not write it up as one: these repositories are created by the test from bytes the test supplies. It is a reproducibility defect, and it is the fixture-side twin of what `.7.2.4` repaired in production.
- Owns: giving the fixtures the same isolated open production now uses, keeping the probe's deliberate `gix::init_bare` and saying in its comment why that one is exempt, and proving the suite's inputs no longer move with a host setting.
- Acceptance: a control drives the existing acquisition fixtures under `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`/`GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0`/`GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0` naming a setting that changes what `gix::init` produces, and shows the fixture unchanged; the probe's own `gix::init_bare` is retained and its exemption is stated in the source; and the twelve acquisition controls pass unchanged.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0208.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCED BY EXTENDING THE CONTROL `.7.2.4` LEFT BEHIND, which is the cheapest reproduction this tree has had.** One line added to `the_git_environment_probe` — build the REAL fixture with `source_repo` and print its `HEAD` — and the same child process that already proved the acquisition refuses the setting printed `acquisition HEAD: ref: refs/heads/main` beside `fixture HEAD: ref: refs/heads/smuggled`. ⭐ The two lines sit in one process under one environment, so the contrast is the measurement: production refuses what the suite's own inputs still accept.
- **The repair.** A single `init_fixture_repo` opens every fixture repository with `gix::open::Options::isolated()`, the same permissions production now uses, and the four `gix::init(...)` sites call it — `source_repo`, the submodule fixture, the LFS fixture and `one_blob_repo`.
- ⛔ **The probe's own `gix::init_bare` is RETAINED, and its exemption is stated where someone would otherwise "fix" it.** The helper's doc comment says it: that first open is the matched pair's other half and has to keep honouring the setting, because a control whose every open refuses the setting cannot tell a refusal from a setting that never arrived. ⚠️ This is the second acceptance clause, and it is a source comment rather than a leaf sentence on purpose — the reader who would break it is reading the file, not the tree.
- **FALSIFIED, self-reversing, proved restored:** reverting `source_repo` alone — ONE of the four sites — to `gix::init(dir)` fails the control (`test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed`), so the control is driven by the fixture the acquisition suites actually use rather than by the helper's mere existence. Restoring and `cmp -s` reports byte-identical; the positive control afterwards is 12 passed / 1 ignored in the acquisition suite and **109 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored** overall.
- ⛔ **CORRECTED by `.11.9.1.3.3` (DOC-0027), and the superseded claim is named rather than edited away.** This leaf's commit published "`SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2` is now closed on every child". That is true of the three children DOC-0026's split produced and FALSE of the goal line they were drawn from, which names "credential forwarding at every redirect and dial" verbatim — a mechanism the split dropped and `.7.2.6` now owns. ⚠️ The error was not the repair; it was reading a split's completeness as a lane's completeness, which is exactly what `MEMORY.md`'s standing warning forbids.
- ⚠️ **Stated at its real width, again:** no assertion moved. The fixtures assert commit ids, file counts, depths and refusal names, and `acquire_local` resolves through the advertised `HEAD`, so nothing was failing. What was wrong is that the suite's INPUTS were a function of the host's git configuration, which is a reproducibility property, not a security one.
- Verification: `python3 -B scripts/project_env.py cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --lib --locked` rc=0, **109 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored**; the acquisition suite is 12 passed / 1 ignored, unchanged. `cargo clippy -p reasonbraid-server --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` rc=0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` rc=0; `make gate` rc=0; `mdbook build docs/book` and `scripts/check_book_links.sh` rc=0.
- ⚠️ **A number in `MEMORY.md` was carried instead of re-derived, by the author of the line that forbids it, and it is corrected here rather than quietly overwritten.** The commits-ahead cell read **133** and was updated to **134** by incrementing it; `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` returned **140** at that moment, so the cell was wrong by six and the edit made it wrong by seven. ⭐ The cell's own sentence says "re-derive, never carry" — the failure was not ignorance of the rule but treating a one-commit-old number as fresh. It now reads the re-derived value, and C1 is unaffected: the blocker is that the remote has never run, not how far ahead the local is.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.7 — The Git acquisition's declared time ceiling is never read

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.15` (REPAIR-0212), while writing `.7.2`'s mechanism table — the mechanism is "bound download/decode/object/**time** consumption before allocation", named in the goal line and carried by no child.
- **The finding, and it is a two-site contrast inside one product.** `git grep -n "max_time" -- crates` returns **five** lines. Three are `fetcher.rs`: declared at `:45`, defaulted to 30 s at `:60`, and **enforced** at `:648` — `tokio::time::timeout(self.limits.max_time, run)`. Two are `git.rs`: declared at `:49`, defaulted to **120 s** at `:61`. There is no third. ⛔ R1's blocking Git transfer has no time bound of any kind, while its own `GitLimits` publishes one.
- ⭐ **Every OTHER ceiling in the same struct is enforced**, which is what makes this a dropped mechanism rather than a design choice: `max_objects` at `:943`, `max_bytes` at `:952`, `max_depth` at `:1012` and `:1032`, `max_files` at `:1059`. One field of six is inert.
- ⚠️ **And the four that ARE enforced trip after the transfer, not before allocation.** `object_count` and `odb_bytes` are both computed from the written object database after `receive(…)` returns, so a remote that sends far more than `max_bytes` has already written it when the refusal fires. The goal line says "before allocation"; this leaf owns whether that clause is met, narrowed, or withdrawn with a reason.
- ⛔ **Also here, from the same table row: there is no decode brake at all.** Word-bounded `ratio` in `git.rs` returns **0**, against `fetcher.rs::check_ratio` at `:828`. ⚠️ The first measurement returned 10 and was a SUBSTRING artefact — `configu-ratio-n`, `ope-ratio-n`, `prepa-ratio-n` — corrected by re-running word-bounded, and recorded because a count from an unbounded grep is not a count.
- ⚠️ **Not reproduced at runtime, and this leaf must not claim otherwise.** What is measured is that the field has no reader and the ceilings run after the transfer. What is NOT measured is a slow or oversized remote holding the worker. Reproduce it first, as `.7.2.2` and `.7.2.6` did.
- Owns: enforcing the declared time ceiling on the blocking transfer, deciding whether the byte and object ceilings can be made to bound the transfer rather than its result (and saying so plainly if they cannot), and deciding whether a decode brake is owed here or whether gix's own pack limits already bound it — measured, not assumed.
- Acceptance: a control observes a transfer exceeding the declared time ceiling and is refused by name, observed RED first; a control observes a legitimate transfer inside the ceiling still succeeding, so the repair is a bound and not a prohibition; the "before allocation" clause is met, narrowed or withdrawn with its reason recorded in the leaf and in the book; and the existing acquisition suites pass unchanged.
- 🔴 **THE DEFECT IS LARGER THAN THE LEAF RECORDED, AND THE WHOLE REFUSAL PATH WAS WIRED AND UNREACHABLE.** The leaf opened on an unread limit field. Re-derived: `GitError::TimedOut` is DECLARED (`crates/reasonbraid-server/src/git.rs:100`), carries a Display message — *"the acquisition exceeded the time ceiling"* (`:158`) — and is mapped to the wire string `timed_out` (`crates/reasonbraid-server/src/api.rs:2646`). `git grep -n 'GitError::TimedOut' -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src/git.rs` returns **no construction site**. ⇒ a refusal existed end to end, in three files, and nothing could ever produce it.
- ⭐ **AND THE HOOK ALREADY EXISTED, WHICH IS WHY THE REPAIR IS SMALL.** `gix`'s `receive` takes a `&AtomicBool` it polls during the transfer; this module handed it `AtomicBool::default()` — a flag nobody could set. ⛔ Census of that shape across the product: `git grep -n 'AtomicBool::default()' -- crates` now returns only this leaf's own doc comment, so the class was exactly one occurrence and it is closed.
- ✅ **THE BOUND IS ON THE TRANSFER, NOT ON THE CALLER'S WAIT, and the difference is the whole design.** A `tokio::time::timeout` around the `spawn_blocking` handle returns on time and leaves the worker transferring. A flag `gix` polls stops the work. The chain, read in the pinned dependency rather than assumed: `receive` → `gix_protocol::fetch` → `gix_pack::Bundle::write_to_directory` → `interrupt::Read` wrapping the pack reader (`gix-features-0.49.1/src/interrupt.rs:106`, which fails the next `read` once the flag is set).
- ⚠️ **THE HONEST SPLIT BETWEEN WHAT THE CONTROL PROVES AND WHAT THE READING PROVES.** The control proves the CHECKPOINT refuses and names the ceiling. The transfer-interrupt property rests on reading the dependency's source; exercising it needs a slow remote, which the leaf explicitly declined to claim and this one does not claim either.
- ⛔ **DECLARED LIMIT, in the source and in the book:** `gix` polls the flag during the pack receive and delta traversal. A remote that stalls in the connection or the ref advertisement is caught by the checkpoint AFTER that phase, so the effective ceiling is `max_time` plus however long one un-polled phase blocks.
- ✅ **THE "BEFORE ALLOCATION" CLAUSE IS NARROWED, WITH THE MEASUREMENT THAT NARROWS IT.** All five other ceilings trip AFTER the transfer: `max_objects` (`:1034`) and `max_bytes` (`:1043`) are computed from the written object database, `max_files` (`:1150`) and `max_depth` (`:1103`, `:1123`) during the tree walk that follows it — every one after `receive` at `:954`. ⇒ the clause now reads: consumption before the first allocation check is bounded **in seconds, not in bytes**, and an operator sizing disk should budget for what the link delivers in `max_time`. Published in `docs/book/src/deployment.md` as a six-row ceiling table with a *when it trips* column, and rendered before it was claimed — mdbook emits 4 cells on every row.
- ⛔ **DECODE BRAKE: DECLINED, on a measurement of the dependency rather than on a judgement.** `grep -rcw 'ratio'` over the whole of `gix-pack 0.74.2` returns nothing — there is no decompression-ratio guard to inherit. But the allocation is FALLIBLE: `out.try_reserve(additional)?` before `out.resize` (`gix-pack-0.74.2/src/data/file/decode/entry.rs:199`), so an absurd declared size yields an allocation error rather than an aborted process. ⇒ a brake of `fetcher.rs::check_ratio`'s shape would duplicate what fallible allocation already does for the single-entry case. ⚠️ What it would NOT duplicate — a pack staying under the allocator's limit per entry while expanding far beyond its wire size in aggregate — is real, unreproduced, and routed to `.7.2.9` rather than guessed at.
- ⛔ **OVERFLOW GUARD: DECLINED, measured.** `Instant::now() + limit` panics on overflow, and the obvious defensive move is `checked_add`. It was not taken because the path is unreachable: `git grep 'GitLimits {'` finds production constructing it only as `GitLimits::default()` (`crates/reasonbraid-server/src/api.rs:557`), and `max_time` appears in no config, environment or request path — every non-default construction is a test. ⭐ Trigger for revisiting, stated rather than left implicit: `max_time` becoming operator-supplied.
- ✅ **THE WATCHDOG DOES NOT OUTLIVE THE ACQUISITION**, which a 120 s ceiling would otherwise cost on every successful clone. `Drop for Deadline` releases it, and `the_watchdog_exits_when_the_acquisition_finishes` holds that.
- ✅ **FALSIFIED IN SITU, AND THE RED NAMES THE ARM.** Restoring the pre-fix behaviour inside the current file — `Deadline::expired()` returning `false`, and `receive` handed `&std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool::default()` again — makes exactly ONE arm fail, by name: `the_time_ceiling_refuses_by_name`, reporting *a zero ceiling must refuse as TimedOut, got Ok(GitAcquisition { … resolved_commit: "8be5445a…", object_count: 4 … })*. ⭐ The acquisition SUCCEEDING under a zero ceiling is the defect stated as an observation rather than as an argument. **14 passed, 1 failed, 1 ignored.** ⚠️ The two arms that pass BOTH ways are LABELLED in the source with the reason: the inside-the-ceiling arm covers the rule’s boundary — its red is a degenerate ceiling that refuses everything, not the pre-fix code that refused nothing — and the watchdog arm covers a resource leak the repair could itself have introduced, whose red is a `Drop` that forgets to release the flag. `cmp -s` reports the restore byte-identical.
- promotion: DECLINED as a note, explicitly per `LESSON-PROMOTION`. The shape — *a refusal wired end to end and constructed by nothing* — is `docs/knowledge/a-prohibition-names-a-mechanism.md`'s neighbourhood and `.11.20.2`'s criterion makes it absorb-or-decline; nothing here is a new mechanism, and the census proving the class is a single occurrence is recorded above rather than generalised.
- Routed OUT: the aggregate-expansion residual the fallible allocation does not cover, `.7.2.9`; and `AcquisitionError.kind` as a second, undocumented refusal vocabulary, `.7.2.10` — found while checking whether this change owed the book a reason code, which it does not.
- NO REGRESSION: no schema, migration or wire contract changed. One struct, one flag handed to `gix` instead of a default, three phase checkpoints, three controls, and a book section.
- lockstep: `README.md` unchanged (objective, layout and standard commands untouched); `docs/book/src/deployment.md` gains the acquisition-ceiling table, which is the user-visible surface this change moves.
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0249`.


#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.9 — A pack can expand far beyond its wire size, and only the clock stops it

- Opened: `pending` by `.7.2.7`, whose decode-brake clause was discharged by measuring the dependency rather than by adding a brake.
- ✅ **What `.7.2.7` established, so this leaf does not re-measure it.** `gix-pack 0.74.2` has NO decompression-ratio guard: `grep -rcw 'ratio'` over the whole crate returns nothing. Decoded sizes come from each entry's self-declared `decompressed_size` (`gix-pack-0.74.2/src/data/file/decode/entry.rs:199`). ⭐ But the allocation is FALLIBLE — `out.try_reserve(additional)?` at `:201` — so a pack declaring an absurd size gets an allocation ERROR, not an aborted process. That is why a brake of `fetcher.rs::check_ratio`'s shape was DECLINED there.
- 🔴 **The residual, which `.7.2.7` named and did not close.** `try_reserve` bounds a single absurd allocation; it does not bound a pack that stays under the allocator's limit on every entry while expanding far beyond its wire size in aggregate. Nothing measures the ratio of bytes received to bytes written.
- ⚠️ **What bounds it today, stated so this leaf starts from the truth**: the time ceiling `.7.2.7` enforced, which `gix` polls during the pack read and the delta traversal, and the object-database byte ceiling — which is measured AFTER the transfer.
- ⛔ **Not reproduced, and this leaf must not claim otherwise.** What is measured is the absence of a ratio guard in the dependency. What is NOT measured is a crafted pack holding a worker, which is what would make this actionable — the same discipline `.7.2.7` inherited from `.7.2.2` and `.7.2.6`.
- Owns: reproducing an expansion that the time ceiling does not adequately bound, or establishing that it cannot exist; and if it can, deciding whether the brake belongs here or in the byte ceiling being made to bound the transfer rather than its result.
- Acceptance: a crafted pack demonstrates the expansion, or the leaf records why one cannot be built and withdraws the concern; any brake proposed is calibrated against legitimate repositories before it is adopted; and the book's acquisition-ceiling table is corrected to match whatever is decided.
- 🔴 **THE CONCERN IS REAL, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THE LEAF WAS OPENED FOR.** `.7.2.7` routed an *aggregate* expansion worry. The measurement found a **single-object** one, and it is sharper: `gix-pack` already refuses to allocate for an object larger than `alloc_limit_bytes` (`gix-pack-0.74.2/src/data/file/decode/entry.rs:475`), and gix ships a **16 MiB** default — `ALLOC_LIMIT_IF_REDUCED_TRUST_DEFAULT`. ⛔ It applies only when `git_dir_trust == Trust::Reduced`, and **`init_opts` sets `git_dir_trust = Some(Trust::Full)` unconditionally** (`gix-0.87.1/src/init.rs:76`). Every acquisition repository this server creates goes through `init_opts`. ⇒ **the brake gix ships was never in force here.**
- ⭐ **AND IT WAS SWITCHED OFF BY A PROPERTY THAT IS OTHERWISE A VIRTUE**, which is why nobody would have found it by reading this project's own code. The repository is fully trusted *because the server created it* — the same fact that makes `open::Options::isolated()` the right config posture — and full trust is exactly what disables the allocation limit. The defect lives in the seam between two correct decisions, in two different codebases.
- **The exposure, stated without overclaiming.** A remote-supplied pack entry declares its own `decompressed_size`; `decoded_object_size` converts it and, with no limit set, returns it; `out.try_reserve(additional)?` then asks the allocator for that much. ⭐ The allocation is FALLIBLE, so this is a large-allocation and memory-pressure vector, **not** an abort — `.7.2.7` established that much and it still holds. What was unbounded is the SIZE a single remote-chosen object may ask for.
- ⛔ **A CRAFTED PACK WAS NOT BUILT, and the leaf says so rather than implying one was.** The acceptance offered *demonstrate it or withdraw the concern*; the measurement took a third route the acceptance did not anticipate — reading the dependency established the bound's existence and the exact condition disabling it, which is stronger evidence than a synthetic pack would have been and does not rest on a fixture nobody will re-run.
- ✅ **THE REPAIR COSTS NOTHING TO REFUSE, which is the argument for this limit rather than gix's 16 MiB.** The limit is set to `max_bytes` — the ceiling this acquisition ALREADY declares for its whole object database. An object larger than the database ceiling could never have passed `max_bytes` anyway, so no acquisition that would have succeeded is refused; an unbounded peak allocation becomes one bounded by a number the project already publishes. ⛔ gix's 16 MiB was rejected for the opposite reason: it is below what this project's own ceilings permit, so it WOULD refuse legitimate content.
- ⭐ **One builder call, on the open the project already customises**: `gix::open::Options::isolated().config_overrides(["gitoxide.objects.allocLimit=<max_bytes>"])`. `isolated()` still loads the repository's own config, and `init_opts` appends its `core.symlinks` override to the same list rather than replacing it, so the two do not collide.
- ✅ **THE CONTROL PROVES THE SETTING LANDS, which is the honest claim** (`docs/knowledge/an-injection-must-be-shown-to-land.md`): `repo.config_snapshot().integer("gitoxide.objects.allocLimit")` resolves to `max_bytes` on an acquisition open. ⛔ What gix DOES with the limit is gix's behaviour, tested by gix; asserting it here would be testing the dependency through a fixture this project cannot maintain.
- ✅ **FALSIFIED IN SITU, AND THE RED NAMES THE ARM.** Removing the `config_overrides` call inside the current file makes exactly ONE arm fail, by name: `the_per_object_allocation_limit_is_in_force`, panicking on *the acquisition sets a per-object allocation limit* — the key simply absent, which is the state every acquisition repository was in. **16 passed, 1 failed, 1 ignored.** ⚠️ The negative arm `a_plain_isolated_open_has_no_allocation_limit` passes BOTH ways and is LABELLED in the source: it asserts the pre-fix state, so the pre-fix code cannot red it; its red is a future `gix` that begins setting a limit by default at full trust, at which point this repair is reconsidered rather than silently duplicated. `cmp -s` reports the restore byte-identical.
- ⚠️ **THE AGGREGATE QUESTION THE LEAF OPENED ON IS NOT CLOSED, and is deliberately not re-routed.** Per-object is now bounded by `max_bytes` and total disk by the same figure after the transfer, with the whole acquisition bounded in time. A pack of many small objects summing past `max_bytes` is refused by the existing ceiling; what remains is only the window between the transfer and that check, which is `.7.2.7`'s narrowed *before allocation* clause and is already published in the book. ⛔ Opening a child for it would be a leaf with nothing left to measure.
- promotion: DECLINED as a note, per `LESSON-PROMOTION`. ⭐ The transferable shape — *a dependency's safety default disabled by a condition your own correct choice sets* — is real and worth a note, but `.11.20.2`'s criterion asks for instances in more than one host before extracting, and this is one. Recorded here and in `DEV_NOTES.md`; the trigger for promoting it is a second instance.
- Routed OUT: none.
- NO REGRESSION: no schema, migration or wire contract changed. One builder call, one extra parameter on a private function, two controls, and the book's ceiling table gains a row.
- lockstep: `README.md` unchanged; `docs/book/src/deployment.md`'s acquisition-ceiling table gains the per-object row and the paragraph explaining why the limit is set explicitly — the operator-visible consequence.
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0251`.


#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.10 — `AcquisitionError.kind` is a second refusal vocabulary, documented nowhere

- Opened: `pending` by `.7.2.7`, which nearly routed a false finding: it assumed the acquisition's refusal strings were §9.8 reason codes and had to check the struct before saying so.
- ⭐ **The distinction, established before anything was claimed.** `AcquisitionError` (`crates/reasonbraid-server/src/resolvers.rs`) carries `kind`, not `code`. The §9.8 registry, `reasonbraid_core::KnownReasonCode` and the book's error table are all about the response body's `code` field. ⇒ `REASON-CODE-DOC` is correct to exclude these, and its census keying on `code:\s*"…"` is correct rather than blind.
- 🔴 **But they ARE wire strings a client branches on, and nothing documents them.** `grep -rn 'acquisition_error\|AcquisitionError' docs/book/src/` returns ONE hit — a JSON example in `deployment.md` showing `"kind":"evidence_unstored"` — with no vocabulary table anywhere. A client author learns a `kind` by receiving one, which is the exact gap `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.7` closed for `code` and left open for this.
- ⚠️ **The population is a population, not a defect count.** `git grep -ohE '=> "[a-z_]+"' -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src` yields **93** distinct string literals, of which the acquisition `kind` vocabulary is one subset among many unrelated mappings. It must be classified before any number is published — `docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md` leg 2.
- Owns: enumerating the `kind` vocabulary from its PRODUCER (the match arms that build an `AcquisitionError`, not a grep over all string literals); deciding whether it is published in the book beside the `code` table or folded into it; and deciding whether a gate is owed or whether `REASON-CODE-DOC`'s shape is simply extended to a second field.
- Acceptance: the vocabulary is derived from the emitting match arms rather than from a literal scan; the 93-literal figure is classified before any of it is published; the disposition names its rejected alternatives; and if a gate is proposed it is calibrated across history first (`.11.6`), with `.11.18.2`'s discriminator applied since `REASON-CODE-DOC` already polices the neighbouring field.
- ✅ **THE VOCABULARY IS DERIVED FROM THE PRODUCERS, AND THE 93 IS PUBLISHED AS NOTHING** (acceptance clauses 1–2). Each `AcquisitionError { kind: … }` construction is walked from its `kind:` line to its `message:` line — 12 sites, all in `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/api.rs` — resolving a local `let kind = match` binding or `FetchError::kind()` where the expression is indirect. ⇒ **41 distinct kinds.** The tree-wide `=> "…"` scan's 93 literals were a POPULATION and are cited nowhere as a count.
- ⭐ **THE INSTRUMENT AGREES WITH THE HAND DERIVATION EXACTLY, which is the only reason its 41 is worth publishing.** The population was worked out by reading the producers, then the tracked instrument was written and returned the same 41 — `TOOLBOX.md`'s *check an instrument's first number against one obtained a different way*.
- 🔴 **THREE KEYS WERE WRONG BEFORE THE FOURTH WAS RIGHT, and all three are pinned as arms.** This is `a-census-is-as-wide-as-its-key` three times in one leaf:

| the key | what it got wrong | the arm that now fires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `kind: match &error {` as a marker | MISSED the `GitError` site, written `kind: match error {` — **16 kinds invisible** | `git-site-is-reached`, `git-site-is-reached-2` |
| `kind:\s*"…"` over the tree | also matched `derived_kind:` and `actor_kind:` — swept in `chunk`, `database`, `approval`, `decision` | `no-stray-chunk` and three siblings |
| a fixed 50-line window | overran `FetchError::kind` into the next item and took the `snake_case` of a `#[serde(rename_all = …)]` | `no-serde-attribute-leak` |

- ✅ **THE DISPOSITION, WITH ITS REJECTED ALTERNATIVES NAMED** (acceptance clause 3):
  - **Publish the list in the book AND gate it.** ✅ CHOSEN. `.11.16`'s rule — *a list nothing derives goes stale* — is satisfied not by omitting the list but by having a gate derive it from the producers on every commit, which is exactly what `REASON-CODE-DOC` does for `code`.
  - **Cite the instrument from the book instead of listing them.** Rejected: the book's reader is a client author, who will not run a census to find out what `kind` they just received. `.11.16` asks whether the owner can PRINT the number; here the owner can, and the gate is where that printing is consumed.
  - **Fold the 41 into the existing `code` table.** Rejected on the measurement that made this a leaf: the vocabularies are **disjoint, 0 shared strings**, and they arrive in different fields. One table would teach a client to look for `timed_out` in `code`, where it never appears.
  - **Extend `REASON-CODE-DOC`'s key to cover both fields.** Rejected: a single verdict cannot say WHICH vocabulary drifted, and the two are produced by unrelated machinery. The arm is separate and names itself.
- ✅ **CALIBRATED, AND `.11.18.2`'s DISCRIMINATOR APPLIES IN THE UNUSUAL DIRECTION** (acceptance clause 4). Over 200 commits, **76** touch a server source and **0** introduce a new kind string — `REASON-CODE-DOC`'s own shape. ⭐ And the zero is REAL rather than survivorship precisely because of the asymmetry this leaf is about: the `code` half has been gated for many commits, so a replay of THAT arm would be worthless, while the `kind` half was policed by nothing at all. The discriminator `.11.18.2` built is what makes the two halves distinguishable instead of one reassuring number.
- ✅ **THE STANDING POPULATION WAS DISCHARGED TO 0 BEFORE THE GATE SHIPPED** — 41 documented, in a book table generated from the producers and ASSERTED equal to them before it was written, so a transcription slip could not survive. Descriptions are derived from each variant's own `Display` message rather than invented.

A client must treat an unrecognised `kind` the way it treats an unrecognised `code` — preserve it, never drop it — and the page now says that.
- ✅ **FIRED RED END TO END IN THE REAL ENFORCER**, not only in the self-test: removing one row from the book takes `scripts/check_doctrines.project.sh` from rc=0 to **rc=1** with `ACQUISITION-KIND-DOC` naming the field, and the book restored byte-identical returns it to rc=0. The rendered page was read back for cell arity — **42 rows, 0 not at 3 cells**.

Three instruments in one session now count instead of asserting.
- promotion: DECLINED as a note, per `LESSON-PROMOTION`. Every mechanism here is already written down — `docs/knowledge/a-census-is-as-wide-as-its-key.md` (three times over), `a-restated-number-needs-a-producer` and `a-control-that-passes-for-an-unrelated-reason`. ⛔ `.11.20.2`'s criterion: nothing new, so absorb-or-decline, and there is nothing to absorb.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.8 — Three ref-verification clauses are owned by the lane and carried by no child

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.15` (REPAIR-0212), from `.7.2`'s mechanism table: "verify supported refs" is named by the goal line, its three clauses are `owned` in the ledger, and no child carries them.
- The three, `R-44-45-4` clauses 1–3, each already measured at the source by tranche 4b and NOT to be re-derived:
  1. **An annotated tag cannot be acquired.** The remote-ref match covers `Ref::Symbolic` and `Ref::Direct` and sends everything else to `_ => return None`, so an advertised annotated tag resolves to nothing and the acquisition reports `NoHeadRef`.
  2. **A short name that is both a branch and a tag resolves arbitrarily.** The short-name arm matches `refs/heads/{requested}` OR `refs/tags/{requested}` inside a `find_map`, so a repository holding both resolves to whichever the remote advertised first — a silent choice between two different commits.
  3. **`refs/heads/..` passes the selector.** `valid_ref_selector` returns EARLY for anything starting with `refs/`, so the `..` guard never sees it.
- ⚠️ Decide (1) deliberately rather than by default: refusing an annotated tag may be the intended policy, in which case the defect is that it reports `NoHeadRef` instead of naming the exclusion. ⛔ Do not "fix" it into a peel without deciding.
- Owns: the three repairs and, for (1), the decision with its reason.
- Acceptance: a control acquires from a repository whose selector names an annotated tag and is either resolved or refused BY NAME, observed RED first; a control drives a repository holding a branch and a tag of one short name and gets a named refusal or a stated precedence, not an arbitrary winner; a control feeds `refs/heads/..` and is refused; and the existing acquisition suites pass unchanged.
- 🔴 **A FOURTH DEFECT, AND IT MADE THE OTHER THREE UNREACHABLE.** `harden_git_url` validates the fragment as the ref selector and returns the URL WITH it; `acquire_into` then passed `url.as_str()` — fragment and all — to `remote_at`. gix was asked to open `…/repo.git#v1.0` as the remote, so **every selector-bearing acquisition failed at the remote**: `TransferFailed("the remote url failed: Could not verify that … is a valid git directory")`. The three clauses this leaf owns all sit downstream of a path nothing could reach.
- ⭐ **AND IT SURVIVED BECAUSE NOTHING EVER DROVE THE FEATURE.** `grep -c 'acquire_local('` returns **13** call sites and not one passes a fragment; the only `#refs/tags/v1.0` in the suite is a `fetch_refspec` UNIT test that never reaches a transport. ⇒ the selector path had no end-to-end control at all. 🔎 This is `TOOLBOX.md`'s argument for controls over readings arriving from the other side: a careful reading found three real defects in unreachable code, and the FIRST control found the reason it was unreachable.
- ✅ **(1) AN ANNOTATED TAG RESOLVES — decided, not defaulted.** An annotated tag advertises as `Ref::Peeled { full_ref_name, tag, object }`; the match covered only `Symbolic`/`Direct` and sent the rest to `_ => None`, so it reported `NoHeadRef` for a ref the remote HAD advertised. ⛔ Refusing by name was the alternative the leaf demanded be weighed, and it loses on the contract: this acquisition exists to produce an immutable commit, an annotated tag is the commonest way to NAME one, and `Peeled` hands over exactly that commit with no peeling of our own. `tag` is deliberately unused — the receipt records the commit, not the wrapper.
- ✅ **(2) AN AMBIGUOUS SHORT NAME IS REFUSED BY NAME, and only when the ambiguity is real.** The old `find_map` returned whichever ref the remote advertised first — a silent choice between two different commits. Now every match is collected and, if they point at DIFFERENT objects, `GitError::AmbiguousRefSelector { selector, names }` names both full refs so the remedy is obvious. ⭐ Two names for the SAME commit are not an ambiguity and still resolve, which is what stops the rule breaking any repository that tags its own branch tip.
- ⛔ **Refusal rather than git's precedence order, deliberately.** `gitrevisions` resolves a short name by trying `refs/tags/` before `refs/heads/`, and following it would have been the least-surprise choice for a CLI. This is not a CLI: the acquisition binds evidence to an immutable commit for a deliberation, and a silent pick between two commits is the exact shape `POSITIONAL-REF` refuses in prose. The caller can always disambiguate by writing the full ref, which the selector grammar already accepts.
- ✅ **(3) `refs/heads/..` IS REFUSED.** `valid_ref_selector`'s `refs/` arm RETURNED EARLY, so the `..` guard eleven lines below never saw a `refs/` selector, and the charset admits `.`. The guard now reaches that arm. ⭐ The negative half is in the same control: `refs/heads/main` and `refs/tags/v1.0.0` still pass, so it is a bound and not a prohibition.
- ✅ **THE GATE THIS SESSION SHIPPED ONE LEAF AGO CAUGHT THIS LEAF.** `ambiguous_ref_selector` is a new `AcquisitionError.kind`, and `ACQUISITION-KIND-DOC` (`.7.2.10`, REPAIR-0250) refused it the moment the wire mapping was added. ⚠️ **Stated exactly, because the mechanism matters and the first wording overstated it**: the gate refused the CHANGE, by command — `python3 -B scripts/census_reason_codes.py --check` — before any commit was attempted. The pre-commit hook never fired, because the check was run by hand first; every commit this session printed `=== all doctrines green ===` before landing. ⭐ A gate catching its own author within the hour is better evidence than its calibration was, and that claim is unaffected.
- ✅ **FALSIFIED IN TWO PASSES, because one could not separate the defects.** Neutralising the three resolution repairs together reds three arms **by name** — `a_refs_selector_carrying_a_parent_traversal_is_refused`, `an_annotated_tag_resolves_to_its_commit`, and `a_short_name_that_is_both_a_branch_and_a_tag_is_refused`, the last reporting `Ok(GitAcquisition { … resolved_commit: "8be5445a…" … })`, the arbitrary winner as an observation rather than an argument. **18 passed, 3 failed.** ⛔ The fragment repair needed its OWN pass: with it neutralised all three selector controls fail at the remote with the production error verbatim, which would have MASKED whether the other three fired for their own reasons. `cmp -s` byte-identical after each.
- ⚠️ `a_branch_and_tag_at_the_same_commit_still_resolve` is LABELLED: it reds under the fragment neutralization along with everything else, but that red is incidental. Its own red is a rule refusing any double match without comparing the commits.
- promotion: DECLINED as a note, per `LESSON-PROMOTION`. ⭐ The transferable shape — *a reading finds defects in code no control reaches, and the first control finds why it was unreachable* — is `TOOLBOX.md`'s tools-first argument already, stated from the other direction; `.11.20.2`'s criterion makes that absorb-or-decline. Recorded in `DEV_NOTES.md`.
- Routed OUT: none. ⭐ `.7.2`'s mechanism table is now fully discharged — "bound download/decode/object/time consumption" by `.7.2.7` and `.7.2.9`, "verify supported refs" here.
- NO REGRESSION: no schema or migration changed. One wire `kind` ADDED (`ambiguous_ref_selector`), documented in the same commit as the gate requires; the selector path's other behaviour is unchanged for every URL without a fragment, which is every acquisition the suite had before this leaf.
- lockstep: `README.md` unchanged; `docs/book/src/errors.md` gains the `ambiguous_ref_selector` row.
- Status: `done`.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0252`.


#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.6 — A credential bound to one origin follows the redirect to another

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.9.1.3.3` (§15: found while classifying tranche 4c and not left unowned). 🔴 **Tranche 4b's third shape, in the lane this session had just declared closed on every child.** `.7.2`'s goal line reads "Validate destinations **and credential forwarding** at every redirect and dial, including numeric IPv4/IPv6 …"; DOC-0026's split produced `.7.2.2` (the redirect policy), `.7.2.3` (the LFS predicate) and `.7.2.4` (the repository open). **None of the three is credential forwarding.**
- ⛔ **The closure claim is CORRECTED rather than edited away.** REPAIR-0208's commit message and live documents say "`SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2` is now closed on every child". That was true of the children the split produced and false of the goal line they were drawn from — which is the precise error `MEMORY.md`'s standing warning names: **count a goal line's mechanisms against the children a split produces**. It cost one commit to relearn, on the very lane whose parent records the lesson.
- The finding, source-measured at HEAD: `fetcher.rs::fetch_with` runs a MANUAL redirect loop with `Policy::none()`, and every iteration rebuilds the request — `if let Some((name, value)) = &extra_header { request_builder = request_builder.header(*name, value); }` — so the header is re-attached on the hop as well as the first dial. `fetch_authenticated` supplies exactly one such header, `Authorization`, and its only production caller is the R5 arm at `api.rs:2182`, which passes a broker-resolved `credential.authorization_header()`.
- ⛔ **So a credential the broker bound to one binding is SENT to whatever host the origin redirects to**, as long as that host passes the destination policy — which every public host does. ⚠️ The hop is re-hardened and re-classified, so this is not an SSRF: the destination is a legitimate public address. What crosses is the SECRET.
- ⚠️ **And the disclosure records the wrong thing, which is the half that makes it hard to notice.** `api.rs` discloses against `document.final_url.host_str()` — the host of the LAST hop. A credential sent to three hosts is disclosed as having been sent to one. The module comment says the credential "attaches for THIS acquisition only (never ambient)", which is true about ambience and silent about origin.
- ⚠️ **Not yet reproduced at runtime, and this leaf must not claim otherwise.** What is measured is the mechanism at three sites — the loop, the header re-attachment and the caller. What is NOT measured is an end-to-end acquisition delivering the header to a second origin. Reproduce it first, as `.7.2.2` did.
- Owns: deciding the rule (drop the credential on any cross-ORIGIN hop, as browsers and `curl --location` do, versus refuse the hop outright), applying it in the one loop that carries `extra_header`, and making the disclosure name every host the credential actually reached rather than the last one.
- Acceptance: a control drives an authenticated fetch through a redirect to a SECOND origin and observes the `Authorization` header arriving there before the repair; after the repair the same control observes it absent (or the hop refused by name, whichever rule is chosen) while the first origin still receives it; a same-origin redirect still carries the credential, so the repair is a rule rather than a prohibition; the disclosure names every host reached; and the existing R0 fetcher suites pass unchanged.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0209.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCED AT RUNTIME, AND THE SECRET ARRIVED — this is no longer a source measurement.** `the_credential_does_not_cross_an_origin_boundary` fails against the unrepaired loop with the origin's OWN record: `[("fetch.test", true), ("second.test", true)]` against the required `[("fetch.test", true), ("second.test", false)]`. The `Authorization` header was delivered to a host the caller never named and the broker never bound.
- ⭐ **THE INSTRUMENT IS TWO HOST NAMES ON ONE LISTENER, and choosing it is most of the fixture work.** An origin is (scheme, host, port), so `fetch.test` and `second.test` both resolving to `127.0.0.1:{port}` is a genuine cross-ORIGIN hop with no second socket, no second port and nothing else changed between the two controls. ⛔ The log records the `Host` header and whether `Authorization` was PRESENT — never its value: a control that prints a credential is a control that leaks one.
- **THE RULE, decided rather than inherited: the credential is bound to the origin the CALLER named and is dropped on a hop that leaves it. The hop is still followed.** ⛔ The rejected alternative is refusing the cross-origin hop outright. It fails closed in the same way, and it breaks the shape this pack exists for — an API that answers with a redirect to a signed URL on a CDN, where the second host needs no credential and the acquisition is legitimate. Browsers and `curl --location` drop `Authorization` on a cross-host redirect for exactly this reason. ⚠️ The consequence is named rather than hidden: a second origin that DOES require the credential now answers `401`, which surfaces as `UnexpectedStatus(401)` — a named status, not a silence.
- **The repair.** `fetch_with` captures `let credential_origin = current.origin();` before the loop and attaches `extra_header` only `if current.origin() == credential_origin`. ⭐ `url::Url::origin()` is the exact predicate — scheme, host and port together — so the rule is the standard one rather than a host-string comparison that a port change would slip past.
- **The disclosure half, which is the part a reader would otherwise never check.** `FetchedDocument` gains `credential_hosts`: the DISTINCT hosts the header was attached to, in order, recorded at the moment of attachment. `api.rs` disclosed `document.final_url.host_str()` — the LAST hop — so a credential sent to one host was disclosed against whichever host the chain happened to end on. It now discloses `credential_hosts.first()` and carries the whole list into the snapshot's `disclosure_policy`. ⭐ The disclosure became a MEASUREMENT of where the secret went instead of an inference from where the fetch stopped.
- ✅ **The module header is true and now says what it does**: it claimed "no ambient credentials" — accurate and silent about the one credential that IS supplied — and now states the origin rule and names `credential_hosts`.
- **FALSIFIED TWICE, in the two directions `docs/knowledge/neutralize-into-the-fix-you-almost-wrote.md` prescribes, and the record earned its keep two commits after being written.** (1) Removing the guard (`if true || …`) reproduces the RED above: `1 passed; 1 failed`. (2) The ALMOST-FIX — `if chain.len() == 1`, "only the first dial carries it", which satisfies the finding's headline and is anchored on the wrong thing — makes the cross-origin control PASS and `a_same_origin_redirect_still_carries_the_credential` FAIL, `right: [("fetch.test", true), ("fetch.test", true)]`. ⭐ Complementary failures, so the two controls bound different halves. Restoring from the pre-neutralization copy: `cmp -s` byte-identical; positive control **111 passed / 0 failed / 1 ignored**.
- ⚠️ **What is NOT claimed.** The rule covers the ONE header `fetch_authenticated` supplies. `fetch`, `fetch_head` and `fetch_admitting` pass `None`, so nothing else in R0 carries a caller secret; and R1's Git transport has its own client, which this repair does not touch.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.2.1 — Isolate Git acquisition scratch ownership

- **CORRECTED census.** The note previously here was wrong in both directions and is superseded. It claimed `git.rs:1164, 1185, 1262, 1305` were production; all four sit after `#[cfg(test)]` at `git.rs:955`, so they are TEST fixtures, and they use four distinct prefixes plus the process id, so they cannot collide with each other — their only defect is §13 locality, writing under an ambient temporary directory. It also MISSED the actual production site.
- The real production instance is `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/git.rs:700`, inside `acquire_blocking`: an ambient temporary directory joined with the process id and a nanosecond field, followed by `create_dir_all`, which succeeds on an existing directory rather than refusing. That is the exact R2 shape `.7.3.3.1` reproduced — an ambient location, a clock used as a uniqueness source measured at about one distinct value per twelve calls, and a create that adopts whatever is already there. Two concurrent R1 acquisitions in one process can therefore clone into one directory, so an acquisition's measurements and receipt could describe another's repository content. This leaf owns repairing it on the repository volume with exclusive creation, as `.7.3.3.3.1` did for R2.
- Why the earlier census missed it: it grepped for the process-id call on a single line, and this call spans several. The third such lesson today — a census keyed on the shape of the last instance finds the last instance. The concept-level census that did find it: `git grep -n "env::temp_dir()" -- '*.rs'` returns 8 sites across 3 files, and a clock-in-a-name search returns the fixtures in `reasonbraid-node` (`src/journal.rs:1330,1780`, both after `#[cfg(test)]` at 1320, plus roughly ten more under `tests/`) which share the `pg_guard` collision shape and remain open.
- Routed from this correction: the ambient-temporary-directory sites are a §13 storage-locality family that no check enforces, and the clock-named node fixtures are the `.11.4.3.1.2.17` family unrepaired in a second crate. Both are owned by `.11.4.3.1.2.21`.

- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0082.
- REPRODUCED, with the production expression run verbatim and the content independently witnessed. 2000 names: **501 distinct, 1499 collisions, and every collision between ADJACENT calls** — so the concurrent case, which shares the process id by construction, is the colliding case. `create_dir_all` on an occupied path returned `Ok(())` with another acquisition's 44-byte pack still present (ADOPTED, not refused), and the production error path's `remove_dir_all` then destroyed it. The ambient temporary directory was measured on a DIFFERENT volume from the checkout.
- A second production defect the census had not named: on SUCCESS nothing removed the directory. The doc comment said "the caller owns its cleanup" and no production caller ever did, so every successful acquisition leaked a bare repository into the ambient store.
- Fix: `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/project_storage.rs` holds the storage rules that `extraction_input` had proved, now shared rather than duplicated, plus `OwnedDirectory` — exclusive creation under `.project-data/<area>`, mode 0700, checked parents, and removal that first proves the path still names the created directory. `GitAcquisition` holds the owner in an `Arc`, so the objects outlive `acquire` for the receipt's digest and the directory goes away when the last holder drops.
- MEASURED, not assumed: an open descriptor pins a directory's inode (0 reuses in 200 create/remove/recreate cycles on the repository volume), but macOS still reports `nlink == 2` on a held descriptor AFTER `rmdir`. So the file owner's link-count check carries no signal for a directory and is deliberately not used; the pinned inode does the work.
- Also repaired here: all five fixture directories in `git.rs`, which the corrected census named as the §13 locality family. They now use the same owner, so the tests exercise the real storage boundary.
- Verification: 97 server lib tests pass, including five new `project_storage` controls — 16 simultaneous creators all live and all distinct, an occupied name refused with the first owner's content intact, a replaced workspace retained with its successor's content intact, repository-derived location on the repository volume, and removal on drop. `.project-data/git` holds 0 leftovers after the suite. Strict `-D warnings` all-targets lint and the rendered book pass.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.7.3.3.4.1 — Drive a successful R2 acquisition through to its snapshot and derivations

- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0095. The stated coverage gap is closed: a successful R2 acquisition now runs through the real HTTP handler to its snapshot and derivations, and the persisted evidence is asserted against the bytes the origin served.

- The seam is a test/deployment profile, not a production relaxation: production constructs a different `Fetcher`, and the shipped https-only public-destination policy is not edited. Follow the established `with_gate` precedent, which is already documented in the source as "the test/deployment seam".
- Acceptance: the control fails against a production-policy fetcher (the loopback refusal it exists to get past), passes with the seam, and asserts digests rather than merely a 200 — a successful acquisition that persisted the wrong bytes must fail it.
- Reproduce: at the predecessor commit `git grep -n "R2_RESOLVER_ID\|r2-extract-worker\|extraction_version" -- 'crates/**/tests/*.rs'` returned two hits, neither an acquisition, and `git grep -n 'acquisition"\]' -- 'crates/**/tests/*.rs'` returned none — the census `.7.3.3.3.2` recorded, unchanged at this commit.
- Fix: `ApiState::with_acquisition` takes the R0 fetcher the acquisition legs use; `with_gate` now delegates to it with the same `Fetcher::new(FetchLimits::default())` it built inline before, so `new`, `with_gate`, `api_router` and `api_router_gated` are behaviourally unchanged and every construction inside the server binary still gets the shipped policy. `api_router_with_acquisition` is the matching router. A caller wanting another destination policy has to write it in its own source.
- The control's shape is three deployments over ONE reference, so each production gate is isolated rather than bundled: `api_router` refuses `scheme_not_allowed`; the origin's scheme with the SHIPPED destination policy refuses `destination_refused` naming `loopback`; the origin's scheme with a loopback-admitting policy acquires. The R2 registry row's `schemes` are widened to the origin's scheme for the three resolves and restored before anything is asserted, so no later suite in the same database inherits it; the control asserts the migration's `["https"]` baseline first.
- Design correction found during implementation: the pre-established design did not account for `resolvers::resolve` filtering on the registry row's `schemes @> [reference.scheme]`. Migration 0027 declares `["https"]`, so an honest `http` reference ranks no R2 pack. The reference's `scheme` is caller-supplied and unvalidated against its locator, so claiming `https` for an `http` locator would have made the control pass on false data; the registry row is a deployment fact and is configured as one instead.
