###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.2.1.3.2 — The projection is verified to EXIST and never to be the proposal's, so an approval for one policy can publish another's bytes

- Opened: `active` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.2.1.2.2`'s decision, which had to ask what a stager actually controls and found that it controls the published CONTENT.
- Reproduce, at the source, three commands:
  - `awk '/^pub async fn stage\(/,/^}/' crates/reasonbraid-server/src/publications.rs | grep -nE "policy_id|policy_version|policy_proposals"` returns **one** line — `SELECT status, tenant_id FROM policy_proposals` — so `stage` never reads the proposal's `policy_id` or `policy_version` at all.
  - Its projection predicate is `WHERE projection_id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2`. Existence and tenant; no correspondence.
  - The decision and the approval ARE each matched to `proposal_id`. The projection — the only reference that carries the BYTES — is the one that is not.
- ⛔ **So the publication pairs an approval with a projection chosen freely from the tenant.** `publish` writes `projection.bytes`; the authority for writing them is the approval of a proposal that names `policy_id` + `policy_version`. Nothing requires the bytes to contain that policy version, or to have anything to do with it.
- 🔴 **That is approval laundering, and it is the project's own headline guarantee** — *"Rust — not an LLM — enforces identity, authorization, ordering, budgets, and publication"* (`README.md`). An approval for policy A can publish the compiled bytes of policy B.
- ⚠️ **And the projection verb is itself unbound**: `git grep -n "policy-projections\"" -- api.rs` is a route whose handler calls no grant predicate, so registering the projection to be laundered needs only enrolment.
- ⭐ **ADR-020 §15.7 step (1) already asks for more than exists**: *"lock the publication aggregate and verify the decision, the approvals, the authority proof, and the IMMUTABLE INPUTS."* The projection is an immutable input, and *verify* must mean more than *exists*.
- ⛔ **What the right invariant IS must be decided, not assumed** (`.11.6`). A projection RESOLVES A SET for a target layer, so *"the projection is the proposal's"* is probably too strong and *"the projection's resolved set CONTAINS the proposal's `(policy_id, policy_version)`"* is the candidate. ⚠️ **The stored row may not be able to answer it**: `policy_projections` holds `target, digest, bytes, unrepresentable, tenant_id` — the resolved `(policy_id, version)` set survives only inside the RENDERED TEXT, so the check may need the resolved set recorded alongside the projection. Measure that before choosing.
- Acceptance: the invariant decided and recorded with the reason, and ADR-020's own wording cited; a control observed RED first in which a publication pairing an approved proposal with a projection that does not carry that proposal's policy version is refused, with the matched pair — the same request against a projection that does carry it — admitted; and whether the projection verb itself needs binding answered explicitly rather than left open.
- Status: `done` — REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0340.
- 🔴 **REPRODUCED LIVE, not argued from the source.** Two registered policies, a projection per policy, an approved proposal for `cp-approved` only — and staging it against `cp-other-proj` returned **200** with `state: staged`. Both projections belong to the same tenant, so tenancy cannot be what separates them; only the correspondence can.
- **THE DECISION: the projection must CARRY the proposal's `(policy_id, policy_version)` in its resolved set.** ⛔ Not *the projection is the proposal's* — that is too strong and would break the artefact's purpose: a projection resolves a SET for a target layer, and a deployment consumes the set. ⚠️ **The residual is ACCEPTED and PUBLISHED**: an approval occasions the publication of a resolved set that INCLUDES it, and the set legitimately carries policies the proposal did not name. What is refused is a set that does not carry it at all.
- ⛔ **WHY A COLUMN RATHER THAN READING THE BYTES, and the naive answer is wrong for a measurable reason.** `render_generic` prints `[policy version]` per clause, so the set looks recoverable from the rendered text. It is not: `render_lock` renders the LOCK rows rather than the clauses, and the compiler DROPS every unrepresentable clause before rendering — so a policy that resolved and whose clauses cannot ride this target leaves **no trace in the text** while being genuinely part of the resolution. A predicate parsed out of the artefact would answer a different question, and answer it differently per target.
- **THE REPAIR** — `migrations/0082` adds the nullable `resolved_policies`; `projections::project` records the distinct `(policy_id, version)` pairs **taken from the resolution, not from the bytes**; `publications::stage`'s proposal read now also yields `policy_id` and `policy_version`, and its projection probe yields the set. `crate::policy::PolicyRef` gains `Serialize` and is reused rather than a second struct being written for one concept.
- ⛔ **AN UNRECORDED SET FAILS CLOSED, and the refusal says which fact it is reporting.** `ProjectionResolvedSetUnrecorded` is a DIFFERENT variant from `ProjectionMissesApprovedPolicy`, because *unrecorded* is not *absent* and an operator has to tell them apart. The disposition is `publications::owned_by`'s, applied rather than re-argued: a governance record that cannot be shown to carry what was approved is worse admitted than frozen. Re-registering the projection unfreezes it and costs one call. ⛔ **No backfill**: the resolved set is a function of the seven-step resolution AT COMPILE TIME, the library has moved since, and re-resolving now would record a set the artefact was not built from — `0081`'s invented-provenance refusal, same reason.
- **ADDRESSED (verified)** — `RB_DEMO=0 bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh policy` -> `test result: ok. 24 passed; 0 failed`, rc=0. Leg A: the foreign projection -> **400**, the message naming both `cp-approved` and `cp-other-proj`, **0 rows written**. Leg B: the matched pair, one field different -> **200**, `state: staged`. Leg C: the same projection with `resolved_policies` set back to NULL -> **400** saying the set is *unrecorded*, not that the policy is absent.
- **FALSIFIED in situ** — `if false && !resolved.iter().any(…)`, the membership test and nothing else, fails leg A by name (`left: 200, right: 400`) with the response carrying `"projection_id":"cp-other-proj"` beside `"proposal_id":"cp-prp"` — the laundering, printed. `publications.rs` restored and confirmed byte-identical with `cmp -s`.
- ⭐ **THE FAIL-CLOSED ARM CAUGHT A FIXTURE THE SAME RUN IT SHIPPED.** `the_staging_verb_requires_an_authority_the_caller_holds` seeds its projection with direct SQL and therefore had no resolved set; leg C of THAT control went red on `records no resolved policy set`. Re-seeded with the set its proposal names — so the fail-closed arm has a live witness beyond its own control, which is the strongest evidence a disposition of this kind gets.
- ⛔ **THE PROJECTION VERB IS DELIBERATELY NOT BOUND, and the acceptance asked for this to be answered rather than left open.** After the correspondence check a projection can no longer be used to publish content outside an approval's own policy, so the laundering path the binding would have narrowed is closed at the join instead of at the door. It also sits in the group the schema census identifies as neither checking nor recording an authority (`.9.2.1.2.2`). ⚠️ **Trigger, so this is a deferral a script could check rather than prose**: if a projection ever becomes consumable by anything that does NOT re-derive the approval join, revisit.
- **NO REGRESSION** — `RB_DEMO=0 bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh policy command_api profiles authority migration_upgrade` -> rc=0, **5 suites, 156 tests, zero failures** (24 + 39 + 63 + 22 + 8), `pg-tests: stopped and removed target/pg-tests/run-41jxrvyq`. `cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --lib` -> `133 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored`. `cargo clippy -p reasonbraid-server --all-targets -- -D warnings` rc=0; `cargo fmt --all -- --check` rc=0; `git diff --check` rc=0; `make gate` green; `make book` rc=0.
- ⚪ **Promotion: declined, and the candidate is named.** *Fail closed on an unanswerable question, and say it is unanswerable rather than answering it* is `publications::owned_by`'s position and `.7.1.2.2`'s, cited here rather than rediscovered. ⚠️ Worth a note if a third instance appears: **a value recoverable from a rendered artefact is not the same value** — the renderer's lossiness (dropped unrepresentables, a different renderer per target) makes the parse answer a neighbouring question. Held per `.11.20`.
- **LOCKSTEP** — `migrations/0082_projection_resolved_policies.sql`, `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/projections.rs`, `src/publications.rs`, `src/policy.rs` (`PolicyRef` gains `Serialize`), `tests/policy.rs`, `docs/tasks/SIGNOFF-REPAIR.md` (this leaf closed, frontier rows, commit log), `docs/TASK_TREE.md` index cell, `docs/book/src/cli.md`, `MEMORY.md`, `LIVE_STATUS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `DEV_NOTES.md`. lockstep: README.md unchanged (it documents no publication verb). lockstep: docs/decisions unchanged — ADR-020 §15.7 step (1) already says *verify … the immutable inputs*, and this leaf performs a standing decision rather than taking a new one.
- Verification: `crates/reasonbraid-server/tests/policy.rs::a_publication_carries_the_policy_its_proposal_was_approved_for` (3 legs, 2 policies, 2 projections, 1 approval).
- Commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0340 (leaf SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.2.1.3.2): a publication carries the policy its proposal was approved for`.

### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3 — Deployment, correction and review lifecycle

- Status: `active`; censused and SPLIT below into `.9.3.1`–`.9.3.3`, because `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.9.1.3.1` measured concrete live defects against three of its five mechanisms and a single leaf would have to qualify all of them at once. ⛔ `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.13`'s ownership repair.
- Sources / owned surfaces: `deployment assignments, drift, corrections, reviews`.
- Goal and acceptance: Bind desired digests/refs to publication, validate receipts and corrective authority, permit subsequent reviews after completed occurrences, enforce waiver constraints, and use relative test clocks with failure visibility.
- ⭐ **ATTACHED CLAUSES, added by tranche 4a** (`R-40-42-5` clause 5 and `R-53-5` clause 3; same ledger). ⚠️ Read the second one BESIDE the `R-53-5` clause 2 row, which locates the cause of the requirement this leaf's goal line already names — they are the same two lines of code.
  1. **The canary wave is a number nothing sequences on** (`R-40-42-5` clause 5). `deployments.rs` stores `wave` as a bare `i64` and no path orders execution by it, so the record's own phrase — "records-only honesty" — is the accurate description of today's contract. ⛔ No part of this goal line names waves or rollout ordering, so a census driven by it reads the column as satisfied by being stored. Decide whether the wave is a SEQUENCER or a LABEL, and say which in the book.
  2. **`schedule_reviews` discards every insert error, so a total storage failure returns a successful empty schedule** (`R-53-5` clause 3). `if inserted.is_ok() { scheduled.push(…) }` is the whole error handling: a primary-key collision, a dead connection and a permission failure are indistinguishable from "nothing was due". ⚠️ The goal line's "permit subsequent reviews after completed occurrences" is about the DEDUPE; this is about what happens when the write fails, and the two share exactly one line of code — so a repair that fixes the dedupe without touching the `is_ok()` leaves the silence behind.
- ⭐ **ATTACHED CLAUSE — a routed-record finding this leaf's goal line does NOT make visible** (`R-75-1` clause 3, tranche 3a; `docs/tasks/artifacts/signoff_review/RECONCILIATION.md`). **That an existing defect id dedupes PERMANENTLY is untested.** The goal line's "permit subsequent reviews after completed occurrences" is about the `(publication, trigger)` pair, which `schedule_reviews` dedupes on `status = 'due'`; this clause is about a different key and a different lifetime, and no control exercises it.
- ⭐ **ATTACHED CLAUSE — a routed-record finding this leaf's goal line does NOT make visible** (`R-33-35-1` clause 2, tranche 4c; same ledger). 🔴 **`deployments::assign` takes no principal, no tenant and no authority field, and the contrast is inside ONE module.** `register_target` calls `crate::authority::grant_held_by(pool, &input.owning_authority, principal)` — this tree's own predicate, put there by `.9.3.1` — while `assign(pool, input)`, the verb that points a deployment target at a publication, has no such parameter and `AssignmentInput` carries no `owning_authority` at all. `record_receipt` is the same shape. ⛔ The goal line's "validate receipts and corrective authority" reads as covering this and does not: a receipt's VALIDITY is not who may record one, and `assign` is neither a receipt nor a correction. ⚠️ `.9.3.1` named `deployments.rs` and repaired the site that HAD an authority field; the sites with no field are a wire-contract change, which is why they are attached here rather than absorbed there.
- ⚠️ **AND a finding this leaf must repair TOGETHER with its clause 4, measured while answering that clause's question** (`R-75-1`, tranche 3a). Neither side of the waiver path consults an expiry: `corrections::record_correction` requires `expires_at` to be present and RFC3339-parseable and never compares it to `now()`, and `reviews::schedule_reviews` selects `WHERE operation = 'waiver'` with no expiry predicate. Two consequences, both live: a waiver that lapsed a year ago still schedules a `repeated_waiver` review for ever, and the trigger named "repeated" fires on the FIRST waiver — one row yields one pair, which `crates/reasonbraid-server/tests/policy.rs:3161` records and asserts. ⛔ A repair that only makes the two hardcoded `2026-09-15` expiries relative would leave both standing.
- Verification: pending; capture the failing case, corrected case, and independent control in this leaf or its children before closure.
- Commit: pending.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.1 — Citing an authority is the same as holding one

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.13`'s ownership repair.
- Reproduce, at the source: `corrections.rs::authority_holds(pool, grant_id)` takes the grant ID **and nothing else**, and asks only `SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM authority_grants WHERE grant_id = $1 AND status = 'active' AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now()))`. It never receives the caller, the action, the selector, the boundary, the publication, or `valid_from`. `record_policy_correction` above it admits on ENROLMENT alone.
- ⛔ So any enrolled principal who can name any active grant records a suspension, a retraction or a waiver in its name. ⭐ The module's own error type for a missing grant is already called `GhostAuthority` — the concept is present and the check is not.
- `deployments.rs` repeats the shape for `owning_authority`, so the repair must cover both or it will be half a repair.
- Owns: binding the cited authority to the authenticated caller AND to the target's action, scope and boundary, on both call sites; and honouring `valid_from` alongside `expires_at`.
- Status: `done` — REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0184.
- 🔴 **THE CENSUS FOUND A THIRD CALL SITE AND A WIDER DEFECT THAN THE LEAF NAMED.** `git grep -n "FROM authority_grants" aee579a -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src/` (pinned to the pre-repair commit, because this repair CHANGED the population) returns **9 sites**, of which **5 ask the grant-validity question** — `corrections`, `deployments`, `lifecycle` and `policy` twice — **in four different spellings**; the other 4 ask different questions. ⛔ The population number was first taken with `src/*.rs`, a glob that does NOT recurse, and it missed `src/authority/selection.rs`. `policy::register` checked `status` alone; `policy::resolve`, `corrections::authority_holds` and `deployments::register_target` added expiry; `lifecycle::record_approval` added expiry AND a subject match. ⛔ **`git grep -n "valid_from"` over those four modules returns rc=1 — NOT ONE of the five consulted it**, though the column is `NOT NULL`, so a grant that had not begun was as good as a live one everywhere. ⭐ And the odd-one-out rule from `docs/knowledge/a-signature-is-a-promise-the-body-must-keep` paid again: the ONE site that bound a subject is the one that had had the attention — and it was still half-bound, matching the grant to `input.approver`, **a string off the wire that nothing tied to the caller**. So a caller could approve AS another principal by naming their grant, which is derivable (`grt_<principal_id>`). That is a THIRD instance of this leaf's own mechanism, named by no leaf, and repairing two of three would have been the "half a repair" this leaf warns about.
- ⛔ **`expires_at IS NULL` was dead in four of the five predicates**: `migrations/0004_authority.sql` declares the column `NOT NULL`. The shared predicate does not reproduce it — carrying it forward would keep teaching the next reader that the column is optional.
- 🔴 **CORRECTION — one acceptance leg is not expressible in the current vocabulary.** *"a grant whose action or boundary does not cover the target is refused"*: `GrantAction` has ten variants, all thread-shaped plus `TenantAdmin`, and `TargetSelector` is `TenantWide | Threads{…}`. `git grep -n "Publication\|DeploymentTarget\|Correction" -- crates/reasonbraid-core/src/authority.rs` returns **rc=1**. A publication, a deployment target and a correction cannot be NAMED by an action or a selector, so there is nothing for a coverage check to compare. Extending two closed vocabularies is a design change, not this leaf's repair; it is opened as `.9.3.4`. The other three legs are met in full.
- **Acceptance, as corrected** — every leg live, and each observed RED first:
  1. A principal in tenant A citing tenant B's active grant is REFUSED on the correction surface, the deployment surface AND the approval surface (the third, found by census).
  2. A grant whose `valid_from` is in the future is refused.
  3. ⛔ *(Superseded — the action/boundary leg, not expressible; see the correction above and `.9.3.4`.)*
  4. The legitimate correction, target and approval still succeed, and a refused correction leaves NO row.
  5. ⭐ A caller citing her OWN grant while attributing the approval to someone else is refused — the link the repair NEEDS because it moved the binding from the claimed approver to the authenticated caller.
- ⭐ **`.9.1`'s asymmetry is settled, and its semantic question deliberately is not.** Both `policy.rs` sites now call the shared `grant_is_live`, so registration no longer accepts a grant the resolver in the same module would refuse. ⛔ Whether a policy's `owning_authority` must be a grant the REGISTRAR holds is a different question — a policy may legitimately be owned by another authority — and stays `.9.1`'s.
- Verification: `crates/reasonbraid-server/tests/policy.rs::citing_an_authority_requires_holding_it`, `bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh policy`. Before: **6 of 9 legs breach**. After: **0**, 12/12. Each arm separately falsified — see the commit-acceptance section.
- Commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0184`.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.4 — An administrative authority cannot name what it is authority OVER

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.1`, whose third acceptance leg asked for something the vocabulary cannot express.
- Measured, not asserted: `GrantAction` has ten variants — nine thread-shaped plus `TenantAdmin` — and `TargetSelector` is `TenantWide | Threads { threads }`. `git grep -n "Publication\|DeploymentTarget\|Correction" -- crates/reasonbraid-core/src/authority.rs` returns **rc=1**.
- So for the administrative surfaces — recording a correction, registering a deployment target, approving a policy — a grant can be bound to its HOLDER (which `.9.3.1` did) but not to its SCOPE: there is no action meaning "may retract a publication" and no selector that can name one. Every such grant is effectively tenant-wide for these verbs.
- ⛔ Do NOT read this as "the administrative surfaces are unauthorized". After `.9.3.1` each requires a live grant HELD BY the caller; what is missing is the narrower question of WHICH publications that authority covers.
- Owns: the decision whether `GrantAction` and `TargetSelector` gain administrative members — and if so, which, since both are closed wire vocabularies and §9.8 publishes a stable registry — and then the coverage checks at the three sites.
- ⚠️ Coordinate with `.11.7.1`, which holds the open question of how the roadmap's published code registry absorbs post-roadmap additions. A new `GrantAction` wire name is the same class of change.
- Acceptance: a decision record naming whether the vocabularies extend and why, with the current variants enumerated by command; and if they do, the new members plus a coverage check at each of the three sites, each control observed RED first.
- Status: `done` — both children closed: `.1` REPAIR-0342 (the vocabulary, the default set and the stored-boundary disposition), `.2` REPAIR-0343 (the coverage check at the five administrative surfaces). ⭐ **The decomposition paid exactly as `.9.2.1`'s did**: the vocabulary landed with the checker extended first and NOTHING depending on it, so the commit that made the narrowing expressible could not break an admission; the commit that made it binding then had one thing to falsify. ⚠️ **What is NOT closed and is said plainly**: a grant is narrowed by VERB and stays tenant-wide by OBJECT — no selector can name a publication — and that residual is DOC-0020's, accepted and published in the book rather than left implied. The DECISION was recorded at `docs/decisions/2026-09-15_the-action-set-extends-the-target-selector-does-not.md` (REASONBRAID-DOC-0020).
- **The decision: `GrantAction` EXTENDS with administrative verbs, `TargetSelector` does NOT, and the extension is a MIGRATION rather than an addition.**
- 🔴 **THIS LEAF'S OWN PREMISE WAS FALSE, AND IT IS THE PREMISE THAT WOULD HAVE DECLINED THE EXTENSION.** The line above says both are "closed wire vocabularies and §9.8 publishes a stable registry" and reads across to `.11.7.1`'s frozen-roadmap hold. §9.8 is the **reason-code** registry — a different vocabulary. `git grep -c "GrantAction\|TargetSelector" ROADMAP.md` returns **0**. The freeze does not reach these types and `.11.7.1` is not a prerequisite; the coupling between the two leaves was the false premise and is dissolved.
- ⭐ **And the project had ALREADY RULED on how to do it**, which the leaf did not consult: `docs/decisions/2026-09-06_authority-boundary.md`, *How to apply* — *"Add an action/ceiling by extending the checker FIRST — a grant that exceeds the boundary must be unrepresentable, not merely unapproved."* So the extension is prescribed, with an ordering constraint the children inherit.
- ⛔ **THE SITE CENSUS IN THIS LEAF WAS STALE AND THIS SESSION IS WHAT STALED IT.** It says "the three sites". Re-derived 2026-09-15: `git grep -n "grant_held_by(\|grant_is_live(" -- ':(glob)crates/reasonbraid-server/src/**'` returns **6** — four `grant_held_by` (`api.rs` serving BOTH publication verbs, `corrections`, `deployments`, `lifecycle`) and two `grant_is_live` (`policy.rs` ×2, a weaker question with the same scope gap). ##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.4.2 — The coverage check at each of the six sites (seven verbs)

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.4`'s decision.
- ⛔ Depends on `.1`: there is nothing to check coverage against until the vocabulary and the boundary carry the new members.
- Owns: the per-site predicate that the held grant's actions COVER the verb being attempted, at all six sites the census names — `api.rs` (**all THREE publication verbs** since `.9.2.1.2.1`; it said two), `corrections`, `deployments`, `lifecycle`, and `policy.rs` ×2.
- ⚠️ **SIX SITES, SEVEN VERBS, and the leaf must not conflate them** — `held_publication_authority` is ONE site serving `effective`, `failed` and `publish`, so a predicate written once there covers three verbs, and any per-verb action must be passed IN rather than derived from the site. ⛔ `.9.2.1.2.1` is the standing reason to check the verb population separately: that leaf found a verb the site census could not see, because the census reads the callers of the predicate and a missing caller leaves no trace.
- ⚠️ The two `policy.rs` sites ask `grant_is_live`, not `grant_held_by`, so they are a DIFFERENT question with the same gap; whether they also gain held-ness is `.9.3.1`'s territory and must not be widened into silently here.
- ⛔ **Holding is not covering, and the distinction is the whole leaf** — `.9.3.1` found "names a grant" and "holds a grant" conflated; this is the third term, and a site that checks holding while claiming scope is the same defect one level up.
- Acceptance: at each of the six sites a control observed RED first in which a held grant whose action set does not cover that verb is refused and a covering one is admitted; and the book's tenant-wide caveat is narrowed to the residual the decision record accepts, rather than deleted.
- Status: `done` — REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0343.
- **REPRODUCE / ISSUE, driven rather than argued.** A live control set the caller's grant to `["thread_contribute"]` — a real registered action, not a nonsense string — and drove all five administrative surfaces. `POST /v1/policy-publications/cv-pub-a/failed` returned **200** with `"state":"failed"`, and the response carried `"owning_authority":"grt_hpr_…"`: the caller HELD the grant and the grant authorized nothing of the kind.
- **ROOT CAUSE (WHY + WHERE)** — `crates/reasonbraid-server/src/authority.rs`: `grant_held_by` asked `SELECT EXISTS (…)` and `grant_is_live` the same, so both answered *this grant is live (and yours)* and neither could answer *and it reaches this verb*. ⛔ Not an omission in `.9.3.1`: until `.9.3.4.1` there was ONE administrative action, so there was no third question to ask.
- **THE FIX** — both predicates return the row's `actions` and decide with `reasonbraid_core::action_covered`. ⛔ **The subsumption rule is NOT restated in SQL.** `actions @> '["tenant_admin"]'::jsonb` would have been shorter and would have made `tenant_admin`-covers-the-five a second definition living in a query string, drifting from the first the moment either moved. `covers()` is the one place the JSON becomes a decision, and it defers.
- ⛔ **A row whose `actions` will not parse covers NOTHING**, and it matches `boundary_from_row`, which returns `None` on the same failure. ⚠️ `Vec<GrantAction>` is strict, so one wire name written by a NEWER build makes the whole grant inert here — fail-closed in the right direction, and stated in the code rather than left to be discovered.
- **`grant_is_live` takes `Option<GrantAction>`, and there is exactly ONE caller entitled to `None`.** `policy::resolve` asks of every LOADED policy's owner whether that authority still stands: no caller is citing it and no verb is being attempted, so there is nothing to cover — and passing an action there would refuse a policy whose owner is perfectly valid. The call site says so in its own comment.
- ⛔ **Registering a policy version gains COVERAGE and not HELD-NESS**, and the distinction is deliberate: coverage is a question about the GRANT, answerable without knowing the caller, so asking it widens nothing. Whether the registrar must HOLD the authority it names stays `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.1`'s, exactly as that site's existing note says.
- **ADDRESSED (verified)** — `RB_DEMO=0 bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh policy` -> `test result: ok. 26 passed; 0 failed`, rc=0. Three arms × five surfaces: an unrelated action REFUSED everywhere; each surface's OWN action alone ADMITTED; `tenant_admin` alone ADMITTED everywhere.
- ⭐ **ARM 3 IS THE DISPOSITION, EXERCISED END TO END OVER REAL ROUTES.** `.9.3.4.1` argued the subsumption in a unit test over a hand-built boundary; this drives a grant carrying literally `["tenant_admin"]` — the shape every pre-change row has — through all five HTTP surfaces. Had it not been honoured, adding the vocabulary would have silently revoked five verbs from every already-enrolled tenant, and no unit test over a constructed boundary would have said so.
- ⭐ **ONE KNOB.** All three arms change exactly one column, `authority_grants.actions`, and nothing else in any request. A difference in outcome can only be the coverage check.
- ⚠️ **EVERY ARM DRIVES FRESH IDS, and the suite is what taught me why.** Four surfaces are one-shot, and the approval is the sharpest: it advances its proposal `decided → approved`, so arm 3's approval against arm 1's proposal was refused *"proposal `cv-prp` is at stage `approved`"* — a STAGE refusal that would have read as a coverage refusal and made the arm pass for the wrong reason. A proposal, decision and publication per arm.

- **NO REGRESSION** — `RB_DEMO=0 bash scripts/run_pg_tests.sh policy authority command_api profiles migration_upgrade administrative_effects enrollment_transaction` -> rc=0, **7 suites, 192 tests, zero failures** (26 + 22 + 39 + 63 + 8 + 25 + 9). `cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --lib` -> `134 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored`. **Whole-workspace** `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` rc=0 — the predicates' signatures changed, so the compiler is the census of their callers. `cargo fmt --all -- --check` rc=0; `git diff --check` rc=0; `make gate` green; `make book` rc=0.
- ⚠️ **WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLOSE.** The book's tenant-wide caveat is NARROWED, not deleted, exactly as the acceptance asked: a grant is now specific about WHICH VERB and remains tenant-wide over its OBJECTS, because no selector can name a publication, a correction or a deployment target. #### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.2 — A publication can be reviewed once, for ever

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.13`'s ownership repair.
- Reproduce, at the source: `reviews::schedule_reviews` builds `review_id = format!("rev_{publication_id}_{trigger}")` — deterministic — and `migrations/0045_policy_reviews.sql:12` makes `review_id` the PRIMARY KEY. The dedupe skips a pair whose review is still `due`; once it is `done` the skip no longer applies, the INSERT collides with the existing key, and **`if inserted.is_ok()`** discards the error. No second review for that pair can ever be scheduled.
- ⛔ The same `is_ok()` discards EVERY insert error, so a total storage failure returns `Ok(vec![])` — a successful empty schedule, indistinguishable from "nothing was due".
- ⛔ And the `repeated_waiver` trigger fires on the FIRST waiver — one row yields one pair — and on waivers that lapsed long ago, because neither `record_correction` nor `schedule_reviews` consults an expiry. Two records reached this independently (`R-75-1` clause 1 and `R-53-5` clause 1).
- Owns: an occurrence-scoped review identity, a real repeated-count threshold with a window, an expiry predicate on the waiver read, and an insert whose failure is reported rather than dropped.
- Acceptance: a second occurrence after a completed review schedules a NEW review; a single waiver does NOT satisfy `repeated_waiver` and the threshold is stated in the book; a lapsed waiver does not trigger; a forced insert failure surfaces as an error rather than an empty success. All observed RED first.
- ⚠️ `policy.rs`'s two hardcoded `expires_at` of `2026-09-15` must become relative clocks in the same commit (`.9.3`'s goal line: "use relative test clocks with failure visibility") — measured 2026-09-14 as NOT yet breaking, and they will the moment this leaf adds the expiry predicate.
- Verification / commit: pending.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.3 — A deployment's declared digest is bound to nothing it deploys

- Opened: `pending` by `SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.13`'s ownership repair.
- Reproduce, at the source: `deployments::assign` validates `is_sha256_hex(&input.desired_digest)` — the SHAPE — and compares it against no publication projection; `tests/policy.rs:2724` assigns `sha256:` followed by sixty-four `a`s with `desired_ref: "abc123"` and asserts 200. The receipt then overwrites the observed state from client-supplied data bound to no node, keeping no history, so a target reports `applied` carrying a digest the publication never had.
- ⚠️ The canary `wave` is a bare `i64` that nothing sequences on — recorded as the current contract rather than as a defect, and the leaf must decide whether the wave is a SEQUENCER or a LABEL and say which in the book.
- Owns: comparing the declared digest and ref against the publication's actual projection at assignment, binding the receipt to the reporting node, retaining what a receipt replaced, and settling the wave's meaning.

#### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.5 — The publication store is BUILT; the gap is that nothing reads it and nothing operates it

- Opened: `pending` by `.11.4.7.2.1.4.1`, whose tranche-1 adjudication returned `fired and open` for the Phase-0 deferral *Git publication reconciliation + object store experiments*.
- 🔴 **THE PREMISE THIS LEAF OPENED WITH IS FALSE AND IS RETRACTED HERE.** It opened as *a publication's immutable content is never written, so the manifest digests nothing outside PostgreSQL*. Both halves of the deferral were run and shipped, in `PHASE-6.4.3.2` and `PHASE-6.4.3.3`, and the audit measured a module name instead of a behaviour. Retracted by `docs/decisions/2026-09-22_the-publication-store-is-built-and-the-gap-is-that-nothing-reads-or-operates-it.md`.
- ⛔ **WHY THE ORIGINAL MEASUREMENT FAILED, so it is not filed as bad luck.** It ran `git grep -n "git::" -- crates/reasonbraid-server/src/publications.rs` → 0 and inferred *a publication is never reconciled against a ref*. The publication module is `publisher::`, not `git::` — `publications.rs:595` calls `crate::publisher::missing_objects` and `api.rs:4061` calls `crate::publisher::publish`. The auditor's SECOND observation (that `git.rs` serves evidence acquisition) was correct; the inference from the first was not. **A grep keyed on one module path is not an absence proof** — the THIRD recorded instance of that class, after `.11.8.2`'s route census and `census_book_coverage.py`'s mention test.
- ✅ **RE-DERIVED THREE INDEPENDENT WAYS** (`docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md` — three different questions, not one pass repeated): **re-derive** — `publisher.rs` implements §15.7 steps **5–8** (staging branch, fetch-back digest re-derivation, write-once immutable ref, compare-and-swap effective channel) on `gix` plumbing; **falsify** — `git log --diff-filter=A` dates it `f53d73d`, **2026-09-08**, *fourteen days BEFORE* the 2026-09-22 audit (`1a87d31`) that called it absent, so the verdict was wrong when made rather than overtaken; **durability** — `cargo test -p reasonbraid-server --test publisher` is **7 passed, 0 failed**, including `the_publisher_writes_the_refs_and_verifies_the_fetch_back`.
- ⚠️ **And the object-store half is not absent either.** `migrations/0028` ships `snapshot_objects (digest TEXT PRIMARY KEY, bytes BYTEA NOT NULL)` — digest-keyed identity, dedup across tenants, and the digest verified against the bytes on write (`DigestMismatch`); `migrations/0080` adds an `external-reference` class for bytes held elsewhere. The CONTRACT §6.3 requires is honoured; only the BACKING is PostgreSQL rather than a blob service.
- ⛔ **NOT the same defect as `.9.3.3`**, and the difference is named rather than assumed: that leaf binds a DEPLOYMENT's declared digest to the publication's projection, one level above this.
- Owns: deciding whether immutable publication content is in scope before G9, and if it is, which store — the roadmap names a Git repository AND a content-addressed object store and the two are different commitments; then binding the manifest digest to whatever is actually written.
- Acceptance: the roadmap's own words for the publication target are quoted with their section, so no store is chosen by preference; the decision names which of the two (or both) and why, with the cost of each stated rather than implied; if built, a published bundle is retrievable by its manifest digest and a control observes a retrieval of content whose digest does NOT match being refused; if deferred again, the deferral names a trigger a later pass can EVALUATE, not a phase that has already closed — which is the defect `.11.4.7.2.1` measured at 27 of 27.
- Status: `done` — REPAIR-0394. ✅ **Every acceptance clause is discharged and the leaf got SMALLER under measurement.** The roadmap is quoted with sections (§6.3 authoritative state, §15.7 the publication protocol, §15.8 the reconciliation matrix, §7.2 the crate map); **both** named stores are KEPT and both already exist; the external object-store BACKING is deferred on a trigger that is two readable facts rather than a milestone — `fetcher::FetchLimits::max_bytes` (today **4 MiB**, `fetcher.rs:59`) raised above **16 MiB**, or `SELECT sum(length(bytes)) FROM snapshot_objects` above **10 GiB**; and the cost of each option is tabulated. ⛔ The *retrievable by manifest digest* clause is the one thing genuinely unmet, and it is a BUILD, so it goes to `.9.3.5.2` rather than being claimed here.
- 🔴 **THE THREE REAL GAPS this leaf found, each now an executable child.** Stated as the corrected picture: the publication store is WRITTEN and well-bound at write time — `api.rs:4053` refuses a publish whose re-composed manifest disagrees with the staged digest, *before* the publisher is called, and the publisher then re-derives the digest from the written blob — but **nothing ever reads it back and nothing ever operates it**.
- Verification / commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0394`. publisher **7/0**; the retraction re-derived three ways, each a different question.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.5.1 — The §15.8 reconciliation matrix is decided and never operated

- Opened: `pending` by `.9.3.5`'s measurement.
- 🔴 **The measurement:** `git grep -n "reconciler::" -- crates` outside `src/reconciler.rs` returns **one** hit — `tests/reconciler.rs:6`. `reconciler::reconcile` is a pure function over (`DbState`, `GitState`, expected object id) → `Action`, all six §15.8 rows exhaustive and 3 unit tests green, and **no production code path constructs a `GitState` or consumes an `Action`.**
- ⚠️ **Why this is a gap and not a style note.** §15.8's own words are *reconciliation is idempotent and regularly exercised under kill points*, and §15.7 step 4 stores *a desired Git operation and an outbox item* — the matrix exists precisely to recover the states that arise when steps 5–8 are interrupted. A publication interrupted between the DB transaction and the ref write is today recovered by nothing; the function that knows what to do is reachable only from a test binary. ROADMAP §7.2 names a `reasonbraid-reconciler` binary that does not exist.
- ⛔ NOT a claim that the matrix's LOGIC is wrong — `.9.3.5` re-derived it as correct and exhaustive. The gap is that it has no caller.
- Owns: observing the real Git state for a publication, driving `reconcile`, and applying the returned `Action` — including the two that must never be automatic (`StopSecurityAlert`, and the failed/later-appearing QUARANTINE, which §15.8 says is *never silently promoted*).
- Acceptance: a publication whose DB row says `staged` while its immutable ref is absent is RECOVERED by the reconciler and not by a human; a conflicting publication id/digest STOPS and raises rather than picking a side; the `failed` row whose write later appears is quarantined and NOT promoted; each action is observed under a kill point injected between the DB transaction and the ref write; and re-running the reconciler over an already-reconciled publication changes nothing (the idempotence §15.8 requires). Observed RED first.
- Status: `done`; DOC-0129 + REPAIR-0401 + REPAIR-0402. Every acceptance clause is discharged by `.2`'s six-case control, and the idempotent re-run is observed. 🔴 **It was SPLIT, because giving the reconciler a caller was not yet possible.** Recorded in `docs/decisions/2026-09-22_a-publication-records-its-git-operation-before-attempting-it.md`. Two prerequisites the leaf did not name:
  - **Nothing records which repository a publication went to.** `repo_path` rides the publish REQUEST; `policy_publications` has no column for it (`git grep -n "repo_path\|repository" -- migrations | grep -i publication` finds none), and `mark_effective` checks the ids against it without storing it. A publication interrupted after its Git write cannot be located.
  - **The commit is not reproducible.** `publisher::publish` stamps it with `Time::now_local_or_utc()`, so the same content published twice yields two commit ids — which makes `RetryStagedWrite`'s own doc (*the same content commits identically*) false and leaves `VerifyAndAdvance` no expected id to compare. `expected_effective` is likewise unrecorded, so a retry cannot redo the CAS.
  - ⭐ Both are what §15.7 step 4 calls the *desired Git operation*, stored BEFORE the write. The code writes first and records after.

| this leaf's mechanism | child |
| --- | --- |
| the desired Git operation recorded before the write; a reproducible commit | `.1` |
| observe → reconcile → apply; the two never-automatic actions; kill points; idempotent re-run; §7.2's binary | `.2` |

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.5.1.1 — A publication is written before anything records where, and its commit cannot be reproduced

- Opened: `pending` by `.9.3.5.1`'s split.
- Owns: the publish verb committing the repository (root-relative, as requested) and the expected effective id BEFORE the first Git object is written; the commit timestamp taken from the publication's staging time so the commit id is a pure function of the record and its content.
- Acceptance: a publish interrupted after its Git write leaves a row that names its repository; publishing the same publication's content twice yields the SAME commit id (observed RED against today's wall-clock stamp first); existing effective rows keep their recorded ids; the book states what the row records.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0401. **A publish records where it is writing before it writes, and its commit is a pure function of the record.**
- [x] **REPRODUCE / ISSUE** — `policy_publications` had no column for the repository; `publisher::publish` stamped commits with `Time::now_local_or_utc()`.
- [x] **CAUSE** — the verb wrote first and recorded after (`mark_effective` stores ids only), against §15.7 step 4's order; the timestamp was chosen at write time because nothing needed the id to be recomputable until a reconciler did.
- [x] **ADDRESSED** — `migrations/0086` adds `repository` (root-relative, §12) and `expected_effective`; `publications::record_git_operation` commits them after the repository is shown to OPEN (`publisher::opens`) and before the first object write, refusing a different operation (`OperationRecorded`) rather than re-pointing it; `publisher::publish` takes the staging time (`staged_at_seconds`, read from `created_at`); `publisher::root_relative`; a store failure is `PublicationError::Storage` → 500, never the caller's fault. `load`/`list` now share one `from_row` instead of two copies of a 10-field destructure. Book: *A publish records where it is writing before it writes* in `cli.md`.
- [x] **NO REGRESSION** — ✅ `publisher` **8/8** (new `the_same_publication_commits_to_the_same_id`); live `policy` **27/27** (the publish test gains leg 1b and a second, deliberately stranded publication); `migration_upgrade` **8/8**; clippy `-D warnings`, fmt, book clean. ⛔ Existing effective rows are untouched.
- 🔴 **AN ORDERING FLAW FOUND BY READING THE TEST, before running it**: recording the operation before the repository OPENS would have pinned the existing *not-a-repository* leg's bogus location, and every correct retry would then be refused. Nothing was written there, so nothing may be recorded — hence `opens` first.
- ✅ **Falsified four ways, each RED on its target, restored byte-identical:** (M1) the commit takes the clock → `the staging time is an input to the id` (the same-id assertion alone would SURVIVE inside one second, which is why the control also checks a different staging time); (M2) nothing recorded → `the row names the repository`; (M3) a different operation overwrites → the retry is not refused; (M4) recorded before the repository opens → `a publish refused before any write records no operation`.
- 🔎 **An observation `.2` must VERIFY, not inherit**: under M3 the retry completed end to end although the immutable ref already existed — with a reproducible commit the retry writes the IDENTICAL commit, and the `MustNotExist` ref edit evidently tolerates an identical value. That would make `RetryStagedWrite` genuinely idempotent; it is an inference from one run until `.2` measures it.
- Commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0401 (leaf SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.5.1.1)`.

##### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.5.2 — A publication's content is written and then readable by nothing

- Opened: `pending` by `.9.3.5`'s measurement; carries that leaf's one unmet acceptance clause.
- 🔴 **The measurement:** the publication surface is exactly four routes — `POST`/`GET /v1/policy-publications` and `POST /v1/policy-publications/{id}/{effective,failed,publish}` (`api.rs:791`–`806`). There is **no read of a bundle at all**: no `GET` by publication id, and nothing addressed by the manifest digest. `StoredPublication` returns the digest and the Git object ids as METADATA; the bytes they name are never served.
- ⚠️ **The digest binds at WRITE and at no other time.** `api.rs:4053` refuses a publish whose re-composed manifest disagrees with the staged digest, and `publisher::publish` re-derives the digest from the blob it just wrote. Both are write-path controls. Nothing re-verifies on the way out, because there is no way out.
- Owns: serving a published bundle by its manifest digest, and refusing to serve content whose digest does not match what the manifest names.
- Acceptance: a published bundle is retrievable by its manifest digest; a retrieval whose stored content does NOT hash to the digest it is requested under is REFUSED with a typed error rather than served with a warning; the read is tenant-bound on the same rule the publication rows already carry; and a control observes the refusal by mutating the stored object rather than by asserting on a constructed error. Observed RED first.
- Status: `done`; REPAIR-0403. **`GET /v1/policy-bundles/{manifest_digest}` serves what an effective publication wrote, verified on the way out.**
- ✅ **The premise re-derived by a different route before building**: the MCP read seam exports a `policy_bundle`, which could have refuted *no read of a bundle at all* — it lists the policy LIBRARY (`crate::policy::list`), not a publication's bytes. The premise holds.
- [x] **REPRODUCE / ISSUE** — the publication surface was four routes, none a read of content; `StoredPublication` returned the digest and object ids as metadata only.
- [x] **CAUSE** — the digest was designed as a WRITE-time control (the publish verb's manifest check, the publisher's fetch-back); nothing read the content back, so nothing could re-verify it, and until REPAIR-0401 nothing recorded where the content was.
- [x] **ADDRESSED** — `publisher::read_publication` (the immutable ref's commit and two files, unverified by design); `publications::serve_bundle`: tenant-bound, effective-only, and TWO checks against the record — the stored manifest must hash to the requested digest, and the stored bundle to the projection digest that verified manifest names; typed `NotPublished`, `BundleUnlocatable`, `BundleIntegrity`; `ControlApiError::publication_conflict` (409, the §9.8 code already in `KnownReasonCode`). Book: *Reading a published bundle* in `policy-lifecycle.md`; `SURFACE-JUDGEMENT` row `policy-bundles covered 1:-`.
- [x] **NO REGRESSION** — ✅ live `policy` **28/28**; clippy `-D warnings`, fmt, book clean; surface census green.
- ✅ **The control MUTATES THE STORE, as the acceptance requires**: the immutable ref is re-pointed at a commit with another manifest, then at one with the true manifest and another bundle (both built by `expected_commit`, objects only); each answers `409` naming the file; the restored ref serves again.
- ✅ **Falsified three ways, each RED, restored byte-identical:** (M1) the manifest not verified → the refusal names the wrong file; (M2) the bundle not verified → the tampered bundle was SERVED `200`; (M3) the tenant predicate dropped → another tenant READ the bundle.
- Commit: `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0403 (leaf SIGNOFF-REPAIR.9.3.5.2)`.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.2.1.3.2.1.1 — I replaced the hand-written LIST and left the SCOPE typed, and the scope was 84% of the bytes

- Opened: `active` by `.11.2.1.3.2.3`'s own preparation. Reading `scripts/run_pg_tests.sh` to price the server conversion showed it builds its clusters under `target/pg-tests` — a directory holding **216 entries** that `census_fixture_population.py` has never once counted.
- 🔴 **THE CENSUS REPORTS 15.9% OF THE BYTES, AND ITS OWN DOCSTRING IS WHERE THE DEFECT LIVES.** It says the families are read *out of the `.join("target/…")` literals in tracked Rust* — and the largest generated fixture families in this repository are created by **Python**. Measured at `028217c`: **1,904,932 KiB across 298 fixtures in 10 Python-derived families**, against the **359,820 KiB** the census publishes. The real population is **6.29x** what it reports.
- 🔴 **`target/pg-tests` ALONE IS 1,309,464 KiB — 3.64x the ENTIRE population the census reports** — followed by `ci-browser` 554,756 / 28, `ci-scanners` 28,760 / 17, `doctrine_scratch` 9,416 / 8, `ci-browser-tests` 1,428 / 21, `ci-workflow-controls` 1,008 / 6, `check-phases` 100 / 2, and three families at 0.
- ⛔ **THIS IS `.11.2.1.3.2.1`'s OWN DEFECT, ONE LEVEL UP, AND I SHIPPED IT IN THE COMMIT THAT FIXED IT.** That leaf found the population 63.1% of the real one because the family list was HAND-WRITTEN, and replaced the list with a derivation. The derivation is correct and the SCOPE it runs over is typed: *tracked Rust*. Deriving membership perfectly from the wrong corpus is not better than a hand list — it is the same error wearing the instrument's authority, which is worse, because the number now looks re-derivable.
- ⭐ **AND THE FIX IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE LAST ONE.** Python has one canonical producer too: `project_env.local_directory(root, "target/<family>")`, which refuses symlinks and cross-volume escapes before creating — the §13 gate for every script. All 10 families come out of it, so the scope extends by adding the Python corpus and its one pattern, not by listing anything.
- ⚠️ **THE SELF-REFERENCE TRAP IS LIVE HERE AND IS CLOSED BY CONSTRUCTION.** `census_fixture_citations.py` and `census_fixture_population.py` carry `target/widget-controls`, `target/gizmo-tests` and `target/pushed-controls` inside their own self-test corpora, as Rust-shaped literals in Python source. Applying the Rust patterns to `.py` files would invent three families out of the censuses' own text — the failure `check_self_tests.sh` recursed on and the family census already hit once on a doc comment. Each corpus is matched by its own language's pattern and only its own.
- ⚠️ **`target/debug` is 67,555,676 KiB and is NOT a fixture family.** It is excluded for a stated reason rather than by a deny-list: `local_directory` is a CREATION idiom, and nothing calls it on `target/debug` — the scripts only read paths beneath it. A rule built on what a producer CREATES does not need to enumerate what cargo owns.
- ⛔ NOT claimed: that any of these families should be deleted. `target/pg-tests` is owned by `.7.3.2.1` and by `census_retained_fixtures.py`'s reduce-never-delete contract, and `run_pg_tests.py` already removes a cluster on SUCCESS. This leaf repairs a MEASUREMENT, not a population.
- Acceptance: the scope covers every corpus that produces a family, derived from each language's own producer idiom; no pattern is applied to a corpus it does not belong to, and the self-test proves that the censuses' own Rust-shaped corpora do not become families; the report states which corpora it reads; every figure this batch published against the old scope is corrected at every site with its superseded value kept; and `target/debug` is excluded by the creation rule rather than by a name.
- 🔴 **AND THE TRAP FIRED ON ME WHILE I WAS CLOSING IT.** Adding the Python corpus made the census read ITS OWN self-test text and publish `python-tests` and `python-nested` as live families — **37 became 39** with no producer anywhere. The corpus-isolation rule, which is the defence I had just written, passed the whole time, because it models the failure instead of running it. ⭐ The fix is derived rather than listed: a file that IMPORTS these patterns is an instrument, not a producer, so it is skipped — and a future census is excluded the moment it is written. ⛔ And the self-test now asserts it against the REAL tree, not a corpus.
- Status: `done`; `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0373`.
- Verification: see the commit acceptance section for this leaf.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.2.1.3.2.1.2 — A producer-derived census is blind to an ORPHAN, and the director's verification is what found it

- Opened: `active` by the director's *ensure your findings still hold*, which `docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md` §4.1 makes the moment a published claim is GRADED. The claim graded here is this batch's own headline — the fixture population — and it is the THIRD time this one number has moved.
- 🔴 **IT DOES NOT HOLD. THE CENSUS IS AT 88.4% OF THE BYTES.** The published figure was re-derived by a route that had never been tried: **filesystem → code**, walking `target/` and asking which directories the census does NOT claim. **13 of them**, holding **303,276 KiB across 440 entries**. `.11.2.1.3.2.1.1` corrected the corpus from Rust-only to Rust+Python and I published the result as *the population*; it was 88.4% of it.
- ⭐ **AND THE TWO ROUTES ANSWER DIFFERENT QUESTIONS, WHICH IS THE REAL FINDING.** Deriving from producers answers *what will accumulate*. Only walking the filesystem answers *what HAS accumulated* — and **a producer-derived census cannot see an orphan by construction**, because the code that made it is gone. No amount of widening the corpus reaches one.
- 🔴 **`target/claude-stubs` IS THE PROOF, AND IT IS THE LARGEST ORPHAN BY COUNT: 270 directories.** `git grep -l claude-stubs` returns **0** — nothing in the tracked tree creates it. Every entry is dated 2026-09-07 and named `refuse-959102000`, `fail-819510000` — the **fractional-second naming `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0085` removed**. It is residue of a producer that no longer exists, and the corpus-widening repair of `.11.2.1.3.2.1.1` could never have found it.
- 🔴 **ONE OF THE THIRTEEN IS LIVE, AND IN A THIRD CORPUS.** `target/demo` — **106,000 KiB / 110 entries**, last written 2026-09-20 — is created by `scripts/demo_two_host.sh:91` (`WORK="$ROOT/target/demo/$RUN_ID"`), a **shell** producer. The census reads `*.rs` and `*.py`. ⛔ That is `.11.2.1.3.2.1.1`'s defect recurring **in its own repair**: I widened the corpus by one language and published the result as complete.
- **The other eleven are historical residue with no live producer**: `checkpoint-ci` 74,692 KiB / 22, three `pg-ephemeral.*`/`pg-iter.*` at 39,4xx KiB each, `probe_1125_1`, `probe_11251`, `probe_1126`, `load`, `rb-cli-e2e-full-flow`, `rb-cli-e2e-denials`, `pg-receipt-control` — all last written between 2026-09-07 and 2026-09-11.
- ⭐ **A DERIVABLE RULE SEPARATES CARGO'S OWN, so the reconciliation needs no deny-list of our making**: a cargo profile directory contains `.fingerprint` (`target/debug` and `target/release` do; no fixture family does), and `doc`/`package` are named by cargo's own published target-directory layout — another tool's contract, not a list of ours.
- Owns: the shell corpus, the filesystem reconciliation, and the correction of every figure this batch published against the incomplete population.
- ⛔ NOT done here: removing a single orphan. `.11.2.1.3.1` established that nothing cited is still present, and removal has never been this lane's act.
- Acceptance: the census answers BOTH questions — what will accumulate, and what has — with the second derived by walking the filesystem rather than the code; cargo's own directories are excluded by a derivable property rather than by our own list; the shell corpus is read; the instrument self-tests both halves; and every figure published against the incomplete population is corrected at every site with its superseded value kept and its commit named.
- ⭐ **THE SHELL CORPUS FORCED THE CARGO BOUNDARY INTO THE OPEN, and its first version was spectacular**: scripts legitimately write `$ROOT/target/debug/rb-server`, so a pattern matching `target/<name>` derived **`debug`** as a fixture family and the census reported **148,813,880 KiB** — the build cache counted as fixtures. `is_cargo_owned` now excludes it by a property rather than a name: a cargo profile directory CONTAINS `.fingerprint`, which `target/debug` and `target/release` do and no fixture family does.
- ✅ **CLOSED. Three independent routes now agree to the KiB**: the census's `families + orphans` = **2,619,172 KiB**, an independent filesystem walk = 2,619,172, and `du -sk` over every non-cargo directory = 2,619,172. The route that found the defect returns **NONE** when re-run.
- ⚠️ promotion: declined (this is a third instance of `docs/knowledge/a-derivation-is-only-as-wide-as-the-corpus-you-read.md`, and the genuinely new half — that no corpus can reach an ORPHAN, so a producer-derived census needs a filesystem-reconciling second half — is added to that record rather than made into a fourth near-duplicate.)
- Status: `done`; `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0377`.
- Verification: see the commit acceptance section for this leaf.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.2.1.3.2.2 — The guard, and the 1,067 fixtures that need no database to prove it

- Opened: `active` by `.11.2.1.3.2`, whose scope `.11.2.1.3.2.1` bounded. The mechanism is the one that leaf named — a guard whose `Drop` removes the directory unless `std::thread::panicking()` — and this leaf builds it once and adopts it where it can be falsified cheaply.
- ⭐ **THE SLICE BOUNDARY IS DERIVED, AND IT IS A CRATE BOUNDARY.** Every one of the 2,375 `journal-tests` fixtures was attributed to the file whose declared name prefix produces it, longest-prefix wins: **1,308 to `reasonbraid-server`** (`tests/node_channel.rs`) and **1,067 to `reasonbraid-node`** (six files), summing to 2,375 exactly with nothing left over. ⛔ `node_channel.rs` requires a live PostgreSQL — its own header says *without `DATABASE_URL` these skip* — so proving a cleanup rule there costs a cluster. The node side needs no database, so it is where the guard is falsified; the server side follows in `.11.2.1.3.2.3` with the mechanism already proved.
- ⚠️ **A per-NAME attribution does not reconcile and was not published.** Summing per-name counts over the helper literals gives 2,392 against a family of 2,375, because two files declare the same prefix and a dynamic `format!("corpus-{index}-…")` name is not a literal at all. The longest-prefix attribution above resolves both and balances to zero. ⛔ Stated rather than quietly corrected, because publishing the first number would have been `.11.2.1.3.2.1`'s own defect one leaf later.
- ⭐ **ONE GUARD, IN THE CRATE THAT ALREADY OWNS THE ROOT.** `reasonbraid_core::fixture` sits beside `repository_root()` — the predicate it must use (§12) — behind a `test-support` feature, so it reaches both crates and ships in neither's release build. ⛔ A copy per suite was refused: a second copy of a removal rule is how one of them stops matching the other.
- ⚠️ **THE HAZARD THIS SHAPE INTRODUCES, STATED BEFORE IT IS TAKEN.** A guard passed as a temporary — `Journal::open(fixture("x").join("node.db"))` — is dropped at the end of that statement, removing the directory while the journal still holds it. Every call site therefore BINDS the guard to a local. The type is `#[must_use]`, which catches a discarded guard but not this shape; what bounds it is that the failure is LOUD — the next database operation fails on a vanished file — rather than a silent pass.
- ⛔ **AND THE CENSUS MUST LEARN THE NEW PRODUCER SHAPE IN THE SAME COMMIT.** `census_fixture_population.py` and `census_fixture_citations.py` derive families from `.join("target/…")` literals; moving that join into the guard would make both report the family as gone. The shared pattern set gains the `Fixture::create("<family>", …)` form with a self-test case, because an instrument that derives from the producer is only correct while it knows every shape the producer has.
- Owns: `reasonbraid_core::fixture`, its `test-support` feature, the family-derivation extension, and the conversion of `reasonbraid-node`'s six `journal-tests` producers.
- ⛔ NOT done here: `reasonbraid-server`'s 1,308, and the other 25 families.
- Acceptance: a passing test removes its own fixture and a failing one retains it, both PRODUCED rather than asserted; the family is measured before and after with the same instrument; `reasonbraid-node`'s suites still pass and strict lint is clean for both crates touched; the census still derives `journal-tests` from the producer after the join moves; no failure evidence and no tracked record is destroyed; and `census_retained_fixtures.py`'s reduce-never-delete contract for the two retained populations is untouched.
- ⭐ **AND THE REFACTOR NEARLY BLINDED THE INSTRUMENT THAT MEASURES IT.** Moving the `target/` join into the guard removed the shape the census derives families from, at fifty sites in one commit: `journal-tests` immediately reported **12** producing call sites instead of 62, and had the last twelve been converted in the same commit it would have reported the family as GONE while 2,375 fixtures sat on disk. The shared pattern set learned `Fixture::create("<family>", …)` in this commit, with a self-test case, and the count returned to 62. ⛔ The lesson is not *keep a list*: a list drifts by one forever and a pattern loses many at a commit you made, which is a signal.
- Status: `done`; `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0371`.
- Verification: see the commit acceptance section for this leaf.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.2.1.3.2.4 — The five families the control run caught growing, and the drop order that decides whether the guard is safe

- Opened: `active` by `.11.2.1.3.2.2`'s own measurement. That leaf's six suite runs added **0** fixtures to the family it converted and **+8,820 KiB / +57** to five it had not, so the next population is not a guess — it is the one the control already caught in the act.
- **The population, derived**: five families produced only by `reasonbraid-node`, **72,368 KiB across 966 fixtures**, and — this is why it is one slice — only **6 call sites**. `cached-decision-tests` 33,604 KiB / 244, `dead-letter-tests` 17,908 / 64, `retry-policy-tests` 16,404 / 84, `codex-stubs` 2,232 / **558**, `identity-persistence` 2,220 / 16. ⛔ None needs a database, which is what separates this from `.11.2.1.3.2.3`.
- ⭐ **THE SHAPE IS DIFFERENT FROM THE LAST LEAF'S, AND THAT IS THE WORK.** In `journal-tests` the helper returned a path the caller used directly. Here each helper's product is CONSUMED by a longer-lived object: `journal_path` feeds `dummy_node(name) -> Node`, and `stub_binary` is passed straight into `CodexCliAdapter::with_binary(…)` as a temporary. The guard has to be handed back alongside, so `dummy_node` returns `(Fixture, Node)` and `stub_binary` returns `(Fixture, PathBuf)`.
- 🔴 **AND THE TUPLE ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT COSMETIC.** Rust drops a `let` statement's bindings in REVERSE declaration order, and the bindings of a tuple pattern count left to right — so `let (node, _fixture)` would drop the FIXTURE FIRST and remove the directory while the `Node` still holds its SQLite file open. `(Fixture, Node)` drops the node first and the guard last. ⛔ The wrong order would very likely still pass on this platform, because POSIX keeps a deleted file readable through an open descriptor; a control that passes for that reason is exactly what `docs/knowledge/a-control-that-passes-for-an-unrelated-reason.md` is about.
- ⚠️ Every call site binds the guard to a NAMED local (`_fixture`), never `let _ =`, which would drop it immediately. `#[must_use]` is satisfied by either, so it does not catch this.
- Owns: the six producers and their 19 call sites — 16 `dummy_node`, 2 `stub_binary`, 1 `fixture_dir`.
- ⛔ NOT done here: `reasonbraid-server`'s 1,308 (`.11.2.1.3.2.3`), which needs a live cluster.
- Acceptance: all five families are guarded and measured before and after by re-running the same suites; the retention half is produced in at least one of these suites rather than inherited from the last leaf; `reasonbraid-node`'s suites pass and strict lint is clean; the drop order is stated where it is relied on; and the census still derives every one of the five families from the producer afterwards.
- ⭐ **THE DROP-ORDER RULE IS NOW ASSERTED RATHER THAN REMEMBERED.** `a_tuple_pattern_drops_its_bindings_right_to_left` records two `Drop`s and gets `["second", "first"]`, so the guard placed first in the tuple is dropped last. It lives in the crate that owns the guard, beside the thing that depends on it, rather than in a comment at nineteen call sites.
- ⚠️ promotion: declined (the finding is a Rust drop-order rule, and it is locked by an executable control in the crate that depends on it — a knowledge record would be a second, weaker copy. The generalizable half, a control that would have passed for an unrelated reason, already has `docs/knowledge/a-control-that-passes-for-an-unrelated-reason.md`.)
- Status: `done`; `REASONBRAID-REPAIR-0372`.
- Verification: see the commit acceptance section for this leaf.

###### SIGNOFF-REPAIR.11.2.1.3.2.5 — The two largest families left, and one test that owns two fixtures at once

- Opened: `active` by `.11.2.1.3.2`, with `journal-tests` fully guarded. The census orders what remains, and the top two are both in `reasonbraid-server`: `cached-decision-live` **35,272 KiB / 411 fixtures** (`tests/node_work.rs`) and `node-replacement` **32,652 KiB / 150** (`tests/node_replacement.rs`) — **67,924 KiB from four call sites**.

Two guards, distinctly named, both alive to the end of the test. Nothing returns them together, so the drop order that `.11.2.1.3.2.4` had to reason about does not arise here; what does is that neither guard may be shadowed or reused.
- ⚠️ Both suites need a live cluster, and they are separate `pg-tests` suites (`node_work`, `node_replacement`), so the verification is two runs rather than one.

- ⛔ NOT done here: the long tail — `r2-join-controls` (in `profiles.rs`, the 8,587-line suite), `conformance-stubs`, `release-tool-controls`, and the `cli-*` families, several of which already carry their own `Drop` guard.
- Acceptance: both families are guarded and measured before and after; both `pg-tests` suites pass against a live cluster with their results consumed and the owned cluster removed; the measurement distinguishes *created and removed* from *never created*, because a flat count cannot; and strict lint is clean.
- 🔴 **THE LIVE RUN FOUND TWO DEFECTS THAT REVIEW HAD NOT, AND BOTH CAME FROM ONE ASSUMPTION: THAT THE TEN `journal_path` HELPERS AGREED.** Nine returned `dir.join("node.db")`; `node_replacement.rs`'s returned **`dir`**, and its call sites append `node.db` themselves — so the mechanical conversion produced `…/node.db/node.db` and the drill died on `SqliteError { code: 14, "unable to open database file" }`. ⛔ Nine agreeing is not ten agreeing, and the name `journal_path` told me nothing: its CONSUMER did (`docs/knowledge/a-fields-name-is-not-its-contract.md`).
- 🔴 **AND THE SECOND WOULD HAVE PANICKED A PASSING CONTROL.** `the_replacement_ritual_recovers_a_lost_node` **deletes its own fixture** at line 463 — `remove_dir_all(&journal_one).expect("the machine burned down")` — because the drill is about a machine that is gone. The guard's `remove()` then found nothing and returned an error, so `Drop` panicked a control for having been thorough. ⭐ `NotFound` on a guard's OWN path is the end state the guard exists to produce, so it is now SUCCESS, with a control that produces the case. ⛔ Not a hole: the path can only be this guard's own.
- ⚠️ promotion: declined (the naming half is `docs/knowledge/a-fields-name-is-not-its-contract.md` — *a field's name is not its contract, its consumer is* — and this is a fresh instance of it rather than a new lesson; the cleanup half is a one-line contract fix now locked by its own control.)
